Hon. J. A. CALDER (Minister of Immigration and Colonization) presented the third report of the special committee on Bill No. 10, an Act to amend the Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment Act, as follows:
Tour committee, in accordance with a resolution adopted at their morning: .session, on Tuesday, 21st of October, recommend that 3,000 extra copies in English, and 1,000 copies in French, of their final report, be printed for distribution, and that Rule 74 relating thereto be suspended.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in connection with this motion I think I should state that the committee working on this Bill had previously arranged for the printing of some 300 copies of our proceedings from day to day. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION TO POSTMASTERS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am
opposed to this Bill for the reason that I think it is very unfair to the postmasters and assistant postmasters who will be affected by it. As I understand it, only nine such officials will be affected, namely, the assistant postmaster at Vancouver and the postmaster and assistant postmaster at New Westminster, Victoria, Moosejaw and Edmonton. I believe that the effect of this Bill will be to continue in force an Order in Council which should never have been passed.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION TO POSTMASTERS.
speechtext:
There are lots like
that.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION TO POSTMASTERS.
speechtext:
As I understand it,
the result of the Order in Council was to reduce the salaries of the postmasters affected to a figure below that which was

paid to them prior to the commencement of the war; and, further, that it had the effect of making these postmasters and assistant 'postmasters refund moneys which had actually been paid to them extending over a period of some two and a half years. I have certain correspondence which sets out the facts more concisely than I could state them, and, with the permission of the House, I intend to read certain of that correspondence. The first letter is dated September 21, 1918, from the Deputy Postmaster General to the Hon. Martin Burrell, Secretary of State:
With further referenoe to the salaries ot postmasters and assistants in certain city offices and especially those at New Westminster and Vancouver, who had been called upon to refund amounts overpaid them during the period of 2J years from 1st April. 1914, I ibeg to say that there appears a misapprehension among these officers and others concerned in the matter in regard to the connection of the War Tax with a reduction in their salaries which called for the refund.
I may explain that the postmasters and assistant postmasters of city offices are paid according to a scale provided in Schedule "B" of the Civil Service Act which fixes the' amount to be paid on certain revenues as follows,

With postage collections of from $40,000 to $60,000-Postmasters $2,200 ; assistant postmasters $1,600.
On postage collections from $500,000 to $800,000-Assistant Postmasters $2,600.
It is only necessary to give these items out of the schedule in dealing with the salaries of the postmasters at New Westminster and Vancouver so that I need not trouble you with quoting all the rest of the figures that belong to the schedule.
For the fiscal year ended 31st March, 1914, the revenue of New Westminster was $43,985, which, according to the scale above quoted, allowed the postmaster $2,200 and the assistant $1,600 and they were paid at that rate. During the year ended 31st March, 1915, however, there was a falling off in, the revenue to $37,419 on which the postmaster and assistant were entitled to only $2,000 and $1,400 a year, respectively.
In the case of Vancouver, the revenue fell from $530,632 during the year ended1 31st March, 1914, to $452,211 during the year ending 31st March, 1915, with a consequent reduction in the amount the assistant postmaster was entitled to, from $2,600 to $2,400.
The War Tax on letters and post cards was hot put into force until the 8th April, 1915. so that it will be observed that the sale of, War Tax stamps did not, in any way, affect the revenue for the year ended 31st March, 1915, during which the falling off in revenue referred to occurred. The revenue collected during these years was all derived from legitimate post office business, and showed that the business at these offices had fallen off to a considerable extent, and the same may be said of all other offices in Western Canada.
There is no doubt whatever that post office business has not regained its former magnitude, but is still far below what it was in 1914. The revenue for the year ended 31st March, 1915, could not be obtained' until July of that year, [Mr, Mc.Ouarrie.1
and it was then found that the falling off of the revenue for the year ended 31st March, 1915, would necessitate a reduction in the salaries of some of the postmasters and assistant postmasters, for the previous year, that is, commencing on the 1st April, 1914. A report to Council was at once prepared for the Postmaster General's signature, recommending that the said reductions be made at once, and if there had been no delay, the officers concerned would only have been called upon to refund over-payments, for one year and1 one-third. There was delay, however, as the then Postmaster General, the late Hon. T. C. Casgrain was reluctant to sign the said recommendation and it was only in October 1916 when he finally concluded that it was not a question of choice, but of statute, that he decided to sign the report to council. If, therefore, the postmasters in these offices are not asked to refund, it would not only be a contravention of the statute, but an injustice to all other postmasters who were compelled to make the refund. Moreover, in view of this being statutory, there is no way the department can relieve them' except by repealing the statute. If the revenue had increased, we would be compelled by statute to give them an increase, and no power could prevent its being given to them. The question of right, therefore, works both ways and the department is compelled to enforce the statute impartially. In consequence of this delay, the salaries of the said officers were not reduced to the amount which the revenue of their respective offices, for the year ended 31st March,
1915,	entitled them to, until the 1st October,
1916,	and the over-payment in each case amounted to $500, that is, at the rate of $200 for 2J years. I wish to emphasize here the fact that the falling off in revenue and subsequent reduction in salaries was in no way effected by the war tax stamps, which were not being sold during the year in which the falling off occurred. The question of excluding the war tax from the revenue begins with the year 1915-16 as it was in April, 1915, that the war tax was imposed. When the revenue for the year ended 31st March, 1916, was made up it was found as it was naturally expected, that, on account of the sale of war tax stamps it had increased enormously. In the case of New Westminster and Vancouver the gross revenues went up to $48,227 and $565,746, respectively. These figures would restore the salaries of the postmaster and assistants to the amount they were receiving in 1914 if the war tax stamps were to be counted as part of the postal revenue. In view of the fact, however, that the Government was taking this means of raising money to carry on the war it was claimed that it would not be fair to the people to impose a tax and then give a percentage to postmasters for simply selling the stamps. This view was expressed to the department both by members and Conservative Associations and as it was obvious that the imposition of the war tax would not entail any additional work in the handling of mail matter it being just as easy to handle a letter with a 3-cent stamp as one with a 2-cent stamp, the department decided that the salaries of the postmasters would continue to be based on the legitimate postal revenue only. The late Mr. Casgrain, who was then Postmaster General, issued instructions that postmasters and assistant postmasters of city offices were not to be allowed salaries on the revenue derived from

the sale of these war tax stamps and from statistics in the department it was calculated that 2S% of the total revenue was derived from the sale of war tax stamps.
The postmasters and assistants had expected to be paid from the gross revenue including war tax stamps sales and it was claimed by them that the department had no legal right to do otherwise. In view of this contention the question of legality was submitted to the Hon. Mr. Doherty in October, 1917, who was then acting Postmaster General for his decision and he referred the matter on to the Department of Justice. The reply of Mr. Newcombe dealing with the question as to whether postmasters are entitled to have their collections from war stamps computed for the purpose of ascertaining their salaries, is as follows:
" I observe that your department has proceeded upon the view that this is not permissible, and possibly that view may be sustained, but I am very doubtful about it upon the construction of the statute. It certainly seems to be a very selfish and unpatriotic procedure on the part of the city postmasters to insist upon taking a share of . this special revenue which is raised not for post office purposes, but in order to defray the expenses of the war; and therefore I suggest that instead of leaving the question to legal opinion you should procure an Order in Council under the War Measures Act declaratory of the intention of the Act of 1915 to exclude the claim of the city postmasters." On receipt of this advice the Deputy Minister of Justice was asked to draw up a recommendation of Council along the lines he suggested and the recommendation as drawn up by him was submitted to council and passed on 8th January, 1918. The order stated " that the Postmaster General considered that it would be incompatible with the spirit intent and purpose of the Special War Revenue Act to permit the diversion of any portion of the special revenue derived from the sale of War tax stamps to any object other than the special one for which such revenue was authorized, viz.: to defray the extraordinary expenses which are incident to Canada's undertakings in connection with the war, and the above recommendation is made in order to remove and to set at rest any doubt upon this subject which might arise upon construction of the statutes."
The question was only submitted to the Acting Postmaster General because of the contention of the officials concerned that the department could not legally withhold from them the percentage based on the revenue derived from the war tax and as the declared policy of the Government was made by the Hon. Mr. Casgrain, Postmaster General, following discussion in the House and representations made by Parliament that none of this money so raised should go into the pockets of postmasters throughout the country, it was decided to refer it to the Acting Postmaster General for a definite decision as to what should be done. It was referred by him to the Deputy Minister of Justice who stated that in order that it might be legal it would be necessary that an Order in Council should be passed under the War Measures Act. It was, therefore, to ascertain whether we could legally do what we had been doing upon the instruction of the Postmaster General rather than to prevent any portion of the money, so far as the officials were concerned, from going to the postmasters, that induced the reference.
I think the above will explain my position and the position of the department in the matter and the Order in Council referred to leaves no doubt as to the policy of the Government in connection with the claim of the postmasters for a percentage of the war tax in fixing their salaries.

I have already, in correspondence with the department, taken exception to the statement of the Deputy Minister of Justice that these postmasters and assistant postmasters were unpatriotic and selfish in endeavouring to get a portion of the revenue derived from this tax. What they were really doing was trying to get from the department the same salary that they had been receiving prior to the war.
We all know that owing to the increase in the cost of living it has been the policy of the Government since the war to increase the salaries of employees in the Civil Service, It seems to me that these men were not asking anything out of the way when they requested, not that their salaries be increased, but that their salaries be allowed to remain the same as they were prior to the war. The Deputy Minister of Justice himself did not attempt to contribute any part of his salary to the purpose of carrying on the war. As I understand it, he received a present of some $10,000 from the Government, and also a very substantial increase in his salary. Had he been desirous of carrying out the principles of patriotism and unselfishness he would have contributed some of his own salary towards carrying on the war, instead of trying to reduce the salaries of postmasters who were receiving $2,200 and assistant postmasters who were receiving only $1,600 a year.
As a matter of fact, although the Order in Council was passed on the principle that none of the money collected from the sale of war tax stamps should go to anything but for the purpose of carrying on the war, the only ones affected by this Order were the postmasters and assistant postmasters whom I mentioned, and the tax did not go to the Government free from any commissions, because the postmasters throughout the country, that is, country postmasters, city sub-postmasters, stamp vendors in the city offices and everybody else who handled these postage stamps were allowed their regular commissions in connection with them. I cannot speak positively as to other offices, but I know that in the case of New Westminster the effect of this Order in Council was to cut down the salary of the postmaster to less than the amounts which were received by two of the clerks in his office. The salary which

was allowed to him under the Order in Council was $2,000, less a repayment of $300, retirement fund payment of $100, and Canadian Patriotic Fund payment of $50, leaving him a net salary of $1,550 a year as compared with the salary of $2,200 which he was receiving before the war. In this office, J. S. Cameron, a 2-A clerk, received after deductions were provided for, a salary of $1,750 a year, and W. H. Bracher also a 2-A clerk, received $1,627 a year. As a matter of fact, the postmaster received very little more than the letter carriers, although he had charge of some forty-five or forty-seven men. That Order in Council was wrong; it should never have been passed. It has been objected to by every member of Parliament in whose constituency any of these officers happen to be and it should not be continued. Instead, this legislation which is now before the House should provide for a return to these postmasters of amounts which were illegally taken away from them. They were illegally taken away from -them, or otherwise there would have been no necessity for the Order in Council. I am certainly opposed to this kind of *thing being continued. I might mention that during last session provision was made for returning one year's deductions to the postmasters, and it seems to me, where the department admitted the principle that a return of one year's deductions was justified, there is absolutely no reason in the world why the Government should not have put through an order for the return of the whole amount, namely, the deductions for two and-a-half years. The postmasters who have been affected by this Order in Council have been unfairly treated, and it is not right and proper for this House, after it has been seized of the facts, to continue in force an unfair Order in Council such as that. I apologize for having taken up so much time, but I feel that I owe it to these men to lay their cases before the House. As a matter of fact, all the members for British Columbia, although they are not all present, would back up everything that I say here to-day. I am not speaking only for myself; they have all written letters to the department, and they are just as much opposed to this Order in Council and its continuance as I am.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION TO POSTMASTERS.
speechtext: The hon. member ought to be opposed to the other Orders in Council also.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION TO POSTMASTERS.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: COMPENSATION TO POSTMASTERS.
speechtext:
If the hon. member exercises his right to reply the debate will be 
closed. Therefore, if any hon. member desires to speak he should do so now.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION TO POSTMASTERS.
speechtext: I have just a few words to say in explanation of the Bill. Hon. gentlemen will remember that in the early days of the war a war stamp tax was levied for the purpose of adding to the revenues of the country. Letters then requiring a two-cent stamp were in future required to bear a three-cent stamp, and many articles were required to bear a stamp of one cent for the purpose of adding to- the revenues of the country, particularly for war purposes, and these taxes were specially designated as war taxes. Later on, under the War Measures Act, an Order in Council was passed declaring that postmasters who were paid a salary on the basis of revenue should not, in calculating their salaries, take into account any of the receipts from the war stamp tax. I do not appreciate the argument of my hon. friend when he says that the salaries of these postmasters were reduced by reason of the Order in Council. Their salaries had beep fixed by statute long before the war, and perhaps I might indicate to the House the principle on whicn they were based. This refers entirely to city post offices. When postage collections exceeded $250,000 the salary was $4,000; when they exceeded $150,000 and did not exceed $200,000, the salary was $3,500; when they exceeded $100,000 and did not exceed $150,000, the salary was $3,250; when the collections were between $60,000 and $80,000, the salary was $2,400; when they were between $20,000 and $40,000, the salary was $2,000, and these salaries were voted annually in the estimates, although when payment was made to such postmasters the exact amount was determined by the actual revenue of the particular post office. Later on the Government was of the opinion that any revenues received by postmasters on account of the sale of war tax stamps should not be considered in calculating what their salaries should be. By reason of the enactment of the War Stamp Tax Act, the salaries of postmasters were not cut down at all; their salaries fell by reason of the diminution of the postal revenue.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION TO POSTMASTERS.
speechtext: In i-ne, days of the war?

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION TO POSTMASTERS.
speechtext:
Yes. That was the reason why their salaries fell, and not because the Order in Council had passed. It strikes me that the policy involved in the Order in Council was absolutely sound. This was a war tax imposed for a special pur-

pose; it did not incur any additional labour on the part of the postmasters, and I think the Government were quite right in expecting that these officers should he tax collectors of this special tax, without any cost to the country. The position of my hon. friend with respect to these postmasters whose salaries have diminished by reason of a declining postal revenue may be all right, and perhaps they are entitled to some consideration, but that does not affect the principle involved in the Bill.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
subsubtopic: COMPENSATION TO POSTMASTERS.
speechtext: Has it been the experience of the country that the increased postage rate has resulted in a diminution of post office business?

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION TO POSTMASTERS.
speechtext: No, I did not say that, but in certain parts of Canada during certain periods of the war, there was a diminution in business generally, which would naturally affect the postal revenue. I am not in a position to say just how matters stand in that respect to-day. This Order in Council will remain operative until peace is declared, which will be shortly, and we are now seeking legislation for making its provisions effective after peace is declared and until the Civil Service classification becomes effective at the beginning of the next fiscal year. I think this is fair legislation and should be accepted by the House.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION TO POSTMASTERS.
speechtext:
What machinery is
there for distinguishing between the ordinary revenue and the special war revenue of the post office?

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION TO POSTMASTERS.
speechtext: The rule adopted under the Order in Council was to calculate 72 per cent of the revenue as being purely postal revenue. The Bill gives power to the Postmaster General to determine what percentage of the postal collections at any post office shall be attributed to the sale of war tax stamps, and the balance will be the amount upon which the salary of the postmaster will be computed. My hon. friend will understand that this must be settled in an arbitrary fashion. To arrive at mathematically correct figures would require a large staff and involve a great deal of work, so power is given to the Postmaster General to settle the matter in the best way he can.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and the House went into Committee on the Bill.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed the adjourned debate on the motion of Hon. Mr. Reid for the second reading of Bill No. 33, respecting the acquisition by His Majesty of the Grand Trunk railway system, and the amendment thereto of Mr. D. D. McKenzie.

subsubtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before entering upon a brief discussion of the Bill on its merits I should like to answer one or two objections that were raised to this legislation yesterday afternoon and evening by speakers on the other side of the House. The hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) positively announced himself as unalterably opposed to public ownership and challenged anybody to give an instance where public ownership had been a success. If he will remain in the House for a short while, I shall give cases where public ownership has been a very pronounced success indeed. He also took the ground that no set of employees would serve a government railway system as efficiently as they would serve a private owned railway. If the employees of the national system of railways were directly under the Government, there might toe some force in his argument, but it is -well to remember that the railways that are now controlled by the Canadian people, and this of course applies to the Grand Trunk if it is taken over, are managed by an able board appointed by Parliament and with powers independent of the Government. The Government has divested itself of power to control, so there is no reason why employees should not serve just as efficiently and just as faithfully under that board as if it were a board managing a private owned railway.
My hon. friend from Wright (Mr. Devlin) made a point yesterday afternoon about the press being opposed to the acquisition of the Grand Trunk. I think he is under a misapprehension. As I read the press, most of the great papers of Canada are supporting the acquisition of the Grand Trunk. I need only mention Toronto, where the three leading newspapers are supporting the proposition regardless of their political predilections, The same thing is practically true of the West, where the great papers are supporting this public ownership idea. My hon. friend also spoke of the Government squandering money, as if we were simply shovel-

ling out money to the Grand Trunk. Surely he has not followed the history of railways in this country or he would know that the country has shovelled out tens of millions almost yearly into the maw of the railway exploiter and got nothing for it. We purpose now to end that practice and to own the Grand Trunk system so that any further money we spend on the road we shall be spending on our own railway. He also referred to the Canadian Pacific, pointing out how magnificently it was paying, and asked why the government-owned railways did not pay. He implied they would never pay. I think I shall be able to give abundant reason before sitting down why the Canadian Pacific railway pays, and pays well. I want to refer briefly to a point or two made by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie), who announced that for his part he was unalterably opposed to public ownership. He also twitted the Government with rushing this legislation through. I cannot help thinking he was ill advised in taking that position. The Administration is not rushing this legislation through. The legislation has been pending for nearly two years, as every hon. member who has read the correspondence in the blueJbook distributed recently must know. If the Government had not pressed this legislation through it would have been absolutely remiss in its duty to this country. The public owned system at the present time is confined largely to the West and to the East, and unless we are able to secure branches and terminals in Central Canada, it is absolutely impossible to make a success of railways under public ownership. Instead of the Government being to blame for introducing and pressing this legislation forward, the Government is to be commended for doing so. We cannot make our present system pay until we get these connections. I do not apprehend, and I am sure hon. gentlemen will agree with md, that there is any rush about this thing at all. Abundance of time is being given and every hon. gentleman who wishes to speak will have an opportunity of doing so. In my judgment the Government would have been remiss in its duty if it had failed to press forward this very important legislation at this moment.
I was struck with an expression of the hon. the leader of the Opposition when he said that the party with which he is associated has nothing to take back or apologize for in regard ito its railway policy. I do not wish to blame one party more than
[Mr. Richardson 1
another in regard to the railway policy pursued in this country for, in my judgment, the country has been on an awful debauch for the last twenty-five or thirty years in regard to its railway policy. But let us examine the railway policy as pursued by the party to which my hon. friend belongs. Surely it must be generally recognized that no greater, no more colossal blunder was ever perpetrated in this or any other country than the building of the Transcontinental railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific at the time they were pressed to conclusion by the party to which my hon. friend belongs. Instead of costing $13,000,000, as was promised, the Transcontinental railway cost, I think, in round figures $150,000,000. It is little or no good to the country at the present- time. I am told that grass and trees are growing up in much of its roadbed. It is away ahead of time. The policy advocated by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Eobert Borden) at that time was in my judgment the correct policy. It was his view, and it was backed by a great .many people throughout the country and by a great many members cf this House, that two or three roads around the north shore of lake Superior were entirely superfluous, that one road was all the country could stand and that (what should be done was to doubletrack the Canadian Pacific around the north shore and let every other railway corporation have running powers over it upon proper terms. That in my judgment would have, been the ideal policy. In addition to the Transcontinental being built, we had the spectacle of the Canadian Northern building around the north shore of lake Superior, and it was this transaction that practically swamped the whole railway situation and brought upon us this crisis.
Let me remind the leader of the Opposition that he surely has nothing particularly to be proud about in regard to the Transcontinental railway, because an independent commission was appointed to inquire into certain matters connected with its construction and they found that $40,000,000 was sjoent either in extravagance or graft on that one road alone. I do not think the hon. gentleman has much reason to be proud of the railway policy of the Liberal party. I am not saying that it is very much worse than the policy which has been pursued by the other party during the last twenty-five or thirty years, because both were thoroughly bad, and now it is out duty as responsible members of the House to apply the only remedy that offers itself

The leader of the Opposition announces himself, I see, as being absolutely opposed to public ownership. He says: "We have not got the money, and if we have not got the money how are we going to buy this Grand Trunk railway?" I do not think the hon. gentleman has a correct appreciation of the situation. It is true that Canada has not got the money to buy the Grand Trunk at the present time, but we do not have to pay for it. We merely assume the bonded and debenture liabilities of the Grand Trunk and pay out of the earnings of the road the interest which they bear. I am in hopes that the course of the arbitration and the terms of submission will be such that we shall not be called upon to pay one cent of the common stock obliga-. tions of the line. If we do not take over the Grand Trunk and assume its debenture and bonded liabilities we are up against the absolute proposition of being obliged to pour tens of millions into this particular corporation in order to maintain it as a running concern. I am told that $90,000,000 is the amount of the obligation of the Grand Trunk to the Grand Trunk Pacific under the contract. The time came when the Grand Trunk reached the end of its tether, they said: "We cannot run this Grand Trunk Pacific any longer," and they threw it up -fell down on the proposition absolutely. Would the leader of the Opposition suggest -and I shall pause for a reply-that the Administration should have stood quietly by, refused to do anything and allowed the thousands and tens of thousands of people who have been induced to go into that country and settle along that line of railway, to remain without any railway accommodation or connection? What would the hon. gentleman suggest?

subsubtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is asking a question of me. He says that this company had reached the end of its tether and had been obliged to go into the hands of a receiver. It has gone into the hands of a receiver, who is the Minister of Railways and Canals. I do not anticipate that there would be any difference if it went into the hands of any other receiver; the business of the road would be carried on in the same way.

subsubtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The Grand Trunk
refused to further operate the Grand Trunk Pacific. The expression that the Grand Trunk was at the end of its tether appears I think in its own correspondence in the Drayton-Acworth report. The Government was obliged to operate the road and if there are deficits on the road it is not due to any
maladministration on the part of the Government which has been obliged to carry this baby, to take care of this child, of the so-called Liberal party. It was forced upon this Government years ago. Surely there is no blame coming to the present Administration on that account. It was simply put up to them and they had to do something with the Grand Trunk because the Grand Trunk announced that they were at the end of their tether and that they could not raise money not only to pay their obligations in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific but even possibly to take care of some of their other obligations.
The Government is faced with the necessity of dealing with the Grand Trunk. My hon. friend says that we cannot afford to take over the Grand Trunk at this time; the fact is we cannot afford not to take it over. In view of the railway situation that Canada is faced with we must take it over in order to save ourselves. I thought the leader of the Opposition was peculiarly unfortunate in the two illustrations which he gave. He said that the position of the Canadian people was like this: They have embarked on the enterprise of public ownership and purchased one cow-I think he said a Jersey cow. Why not, he asked, let us see whether we can make a success out of this cow before we buy another? Well, Mr. Speaker, it seemed to me that my hon. friend utterly failed to grasp the idea that the cow we had bought or rather that was forced upon us was a dry cow-it does not yield any milk. In order to make that cow productive, he inquired, would you go on and buy another cow. I say yes; we want to get a mate for the cow we have bought and see if we cannot put the pair in the way of producing for ourselves milk, butter and cheese. We will never get these products until we have another cow associated with the one we have bought and make the two productive. I think that is clear. My hon. friend also used another parallel which I thought was most unfortunate when he said the country is in the position of purchasing a horse-the hon. gentleman seems to have a peculiar affection for domestic animals-and when we come to make the purchase, he says, we find a bill of sale, or liens, on the horse. Now that is perfectly true. The horse is there, we have got to purchase it, and if we do not make the purchase we have got to pay the liens and the bill of sale, anyway. That is the position with regard to the railroads of this country; I want to make that point as clear as I can. Now

I would like to give a few figures, and I will endeavour to be as brief as possible, in order to show what this country has done for the railroads of the Dominion. I prefaced my remarks by stating, and I challenge contradiction, that the people of Canada during the last forty or fifty years have given sufficient-and I want this to sink into the mind of every hon. gentleman here-have given sufficient in cash, and lands, and the equivalent, to build every mile of railroad that we have in the Dominion at the present time. That is true; the people of Canada have given sufficient in cash, land, completed roads, exemptions, and largesse of one kind and another, to build every mile of railroad that now exists in Canada. And we do not own the railroads-in fact, for the last twenty, thirty, or forty years they have practically owned us. Now let us see where we would have been had we started on the right line? We have paid this money, we have given these exemptions, we have given this land, and yet, had we built and owned the railroads ourselves, we would have had them all paid for and there would be no capital to provide interest on. But because we have dealt with the buccaneers, manipulators, and railroad exploiters for the last thirty or forty years, we have this enormous railroad mileage in existence at the present time. It has all been loaded with stocks and bonds to the value of every dollar they cost and more, and the country has got to pay in freight rates sufficient to provide for the interest on this vast amount of capitalization. Had we done the thing ourselves we would never have been called upon to pay anything like the rates that we are now paying. I remember reading, when I was rather a young lad, and the Canadian Pacific Railway charter was before Parliament, that Sir John Macdonald, the man who was the father of that railway, made the statement that owing to the vast subsidies which the people of Canada were giving to the Canadian Pacific they would be able to carry freight at about one-half what they would be obliged to charge if they built the road with their own money. Now, notwithstanding the fact that we have *poured this enormous sum of money, much exceeding a billion, into the construction of all these railroads we are obliged to pay the very highest freight rates at the present time; and the carnival will continue unless a halt is called. I admit it is late in the day, very late. This carnival has not existed with my aequiesence, because I began twenty-five years ago to denounce it, 
and use my influence to turn, the people away from the idea of pouring subsidies into railway corporations. But it has gone on and we are face to face with this difficulty; and I ask hon. gentlemen opposite who expect to vote against this arrangement to pause and consider what the alternative is: you must either take over the Grand Trunk or continue to pour tens of millions of dollars into the maw of these corporations. That is the alternative, and the only alternative, because w'e are told this railway company are at the end of their tether.

subsubtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Would it not be possible for the Government to simply let the Grand Trunk go info liquidation?

subsubtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Well, that could be done, but one of the great difficulties about the Grand Trunk, I may tell my hon. friend, is that it is a vast system and a great portion of it is in the United States and there are complications-so I am informed in discussing the matter with experts-that make it almost impossible to resort to that expedient. The view is held by the men who are in a position to know, the men who have studied questions of this kind, that the only possible way, the only satisfactory way, by which this road can be acquired is in the manner that, the Government has adopted. For a long time I held the view suggested by my hon. friend (Mr. Cannon). If there is one thing that I feel, and feel strongly, it is that this country owes nothing, absolutely nothing, to any railroad corporation,. All these corporations have held the people by the throat for many years and have shaken the last dollar out of them. Talk of generosity! I would not extend one atom of generosity to railway exploiters. They have exercised a malign influence in this Dominion for the last thirty or forty years. Their course and their machinations for decades have resulted in debauching the people of Canada and I feel no generosity towards them. I would exact the last dollar, and I am hopeful-it is my view in supporting this arbitration-that the terms of the arbitration will be such that the idea of generosity will not even be thought of. The manipulators of the stock of the Grand Trunk have been making money all these years out of these manipulations. Is it not time we came to the end of this flim-flam game? Is it not time we heard the last of the talk we have heard with respect to the credit of Canada that has been dealt out to us during the last fifteen or twenty years? Whenever a crisis arose in this country and there was

any idea of the people doing justice to themselves-doing justice to themselves and even no injustice to the party of the second part-you always heard the view expressed: " Oh, the credit of Canada will be interfered with." What do we care about that? Let us interfere with the credit of Canada. If that credit is to buttress up all these crawling creatures and has got to suffer because of their machinations, as jt has suffered for decades, it is time we'said: " To Hades with the credit of Canada." The time has come when we are not looking to British capital as the source from which to derive our money in this country. Because we have found that we must rely upon ourselves. We have to pay the piper, and the commitments of this country are appalling-appalling is the word-and we should see to it that not one farthing beyond a just award is paid for this Grand Trunk system. I would like to see .provision made that the award be reviewed by Parliament.

subsubtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I appreciate that view as expressed by an hon. member of the Opposition. I do not know whether or not it is feasible, but I have the assurance not perhaps on behalf of the Government, but from a Government source, that in this arbitration the selling value of the stock in the old land will not be considered or allowed to influence the award and I have the further assurance that the obligations of the Grand Trunk to the Government under the Grand Trunk Pacific contract will be provided for. Naturally I felt considerable uneasiness, coupled with some indignation, when I saw in the newspapers that stock jobbers were manipulating the Grand Trunk stock in the Old Land, and that it would influence the price we must pay. The report went out broadcast that this was a stock jobbers' deal, and that perhaps men who if they got their desserts should be in the penitentiary, would make big profits out of this transaction. I carried my fears to a Government source, and I was assured that not one farthing would be added to any award because of any supposed selling value of the stock in London.

subsubtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend
permit me a question? Can he tell this House any method by which the arbitrators can be prevented from giving value to the stock by recognizing what it is selling for in London? How can that be prevented, and how would the award stand if the arbitrators refused to recognize such value?

subsubtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I could not tell my hon. friend off-hand just how it could be prevented. But if I were an arbitrator- and I hope to see an able layman on that arbitration and not a technical judge-I certainly would not award a single cent because of any manipulation of the stock in London. I do not know exactly how that can be done, but I give my hon. friend the opinion that I have obtained.
I have no quarrel with the leader of the Opposition because of the opinions he holds. Yesterday he frankly stated that he was opposed to public ownership. He appealed to his long public record, and if he is honestly convinced that public ownership is an improper thing for this country, he has an absolute right to that view, and I duly respect it and him for stating it frankly. I take the other view, however, and I advocate public ownership as strongly as I know how. I am extremely anxious that this great transaction should be closed up. I believe its consummation will mean a great deal for Canada, and therefore I am not in favour of delay. But I agree with hon. members on the Opposition side who suggest that every possible safeguard should be thrown around this transaction in order that the country shall not be bled to the extent of even one farthing beyond what is the just and proper amount to be paid for the acquisition of this railway.
Mr. JEAN J. DENIS (Joliette): Will my hon. friend allow me a friendly question? I may say that he is making many friends on this side of the House, at least as far as I and many members to whom I have spoken are concerned, when he says that the country owes nothing to the railroads, that we have no generosity to extend to them, and no presents to give them. But our great apprehension on this side of the House is that the award to be made by the arbitrators may constitute a most magnificent present to the Grand Trunk Company by reason of the fact that these arbitrators are liable to make mistakes on a large scale in the valuation of such an immense transaction as this, and that if the award is final there will be no appeal from it either to the Supreme Court of Canada, to the Privy Council, to the Parliament of Canada, or to any other tribunal in the world. If the arbitrators should place a value of, say, $50,000,000 in excess of the real value of the stock, then we would have to pay the excess. Therefore my question is this: Would not the hon. gentleman agree with us on this side of the House

when we say that the award should be submitted to Parliament before it becomes final and valid?

subsubtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I might say in reply to my hon. friend, that I greatly ap-, preciate the position which some members on the Opposition side appear to desire to take on this question. I do think, however, that they are seriously misled, but I am not impugning their motives. If at were feasible that the award should be submitted to Parliament, I would certainly like to see it presented to us for ratification; but there might be difficulties in taking such a course, and I would not like to answer off-hand the question put by my hon. friend. We shall probably hear from the Government on that point.
I want to see the arbitration agreement, for I think it should receive the attention of the House, and I would like to see it submitted to the House when we go into committee on the Bill, because this is a very important matter. All classes of politicians in this House are equally to blame for our present railway situation, and the time has come when we might very well say: Let us look at this question on its merits, and on its merits alone. Let us see whether it is desirable that this railway should be taken over, and let us not be influenced by partisan considerations in reaching a conclusion. Partisan considerations have been the great curse of this country for the last thirty or forty years, and we now see the handwriting on the wall. The people themselves have begun to realize that partisanship is a curse, and 'they are taking the game into their own hands. I am not prepared to say that it might not be a good thing, if we, the people's representatives, will not apply the reform that the people themselves, should speak and act. What difference will it make if the Union Government and the so-called Liberal party be set aside, so long as the people are truly served ? That should be the only issue to be considered in the Dominion at the present time.

subsubtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Would it not be a good idea to let them speak on this question through a general election?

subsubtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I promised to present a very brief summary of what the Dominion has given to the railroads, and when I refer first to the Canadian Pacific railway my hon. friend from Wright (Mr. Devlin) will see the answer to his question: Why cannot the Government-owned railway pay

as well as the Canadian Pacific railway? First, let me give a brief historical reference 1 have in mind, and in this connection I would like to appeal to my hon. friends on the Opposition side. In the year 1872 the Mackenzie Government came into office, led by as grand a man and Liberal as ever appeared in this country. He was the man who helped to create the great Liberal party, and he believed in public ownership. That grand old Scotchman had made a study of the question, and he realized Canada's needs and necessities, and he advocated that the railway system to bind the East to the West, which was a condition of Confederation, should be built under public ownership.
It would have been a great thing for this Dominion had the hon. Alexander Mackenzie been continued in power long enough to carry out that policy. It would have saved hundreds of millions of dollars to the people of this country, it would have meant decent freight rates, and we would not have had the bedevilment and corruption of our politics and public life that we have witnessed during the last thirty or forty years. I -want to appeal especially to my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie). His honoured leader, the man who helped to create his party, believed in public ownership and undertook the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway to connect the Pacific with the Atlantic as a publicly-owned line.
His party continued in office, as is well known, from 1872 until 1878, when it was defeated on the trade question-an improper issue at that time, as history will attest. But he was defeated, and Sir John A. Macdonald, the great apostle of private ownership, came into office. And what did he do? He brought into existence the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and handed over to it at once $38,000,000 worth of road that had been completed under Mackenzie and
25,000,000 acres of land. Let us see what the Canadian Pacific Railway Company actually received. They got $71,000,000 in cash. They got $38,000,000 worth of completed road. They got a land grant running up to some thirty or thirty-five million acres. Now, they have realized over $125,000,000 from the land which they have sold, and, according to their own statement, the land which still remains, untaxed, in their hands they value at another $125,000,000. So that the people gave them directly-it was just the same as cash-$359,000,000. And the original cost of the road, according to their own figures, was $143,000,000.

Let us examine what further aid they received. They got exemption from duty on all their supplies. They got exemption from taxation until Gabriel blows his trumpet on every penny's worth of property that they own in this country. Do you know what that means? If you figure it out according to recognized authorities you will find that that means $500,000,000 to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company every thirty years. As the company have been in existence over thirty years, the people, therefore, have contributed to the Canadian Pacific Company about $850,000,000 in cash, lands and tax exemptions. No wonder they can earn splendid dividends; no wonder they can set aside a handsome reserve of from one hundred to twp hundred millions.
I commend the figures to my hon. friend the member for Wright (Mr. Devlin). It is in order to combat the strength of that great railway company that we want to have the [DOT] Canadian-owned system strengthened; because I believe our system will be able to compete satisfactorily with the Canadian Pacific (when the time comes if we get it properly organized and co-ordinated.
Now, let us see what we gave to the Canadian Northern. I want my hon. friend (Mr. Denis) to listen to this, because it is important; he has a receptive mind and I am satisfied that his vote on this question will be an honest one.
Mark you, we gave $850,000,000 to the Canadian Pacific, and into the maw of the Canadian Northern the people of Canada poured $300,000,000. Is it any wonder that there has been a bedevilment of our politics in this country? Is it any wonder that the great railway interests became arrogant and overbearing and practically attempted to own the country as they gained in affluence and wealth?
According to the information given by the Minister of Railways this afternoon, we gave to the Grand Trunk $15,000,000. Mark you, the people gave $674,000,000 in cash or its equivalent to the three railroads of this country; and if you add $500,000,000 by way of tax exemption and duty exemption you will get the enormous total of $1,540,000,000 that the people of Canada have contributed to the railroads of this country.
If that is not sufficient to appal members of Parliament, to say nothing of the citizens ot Canada-well, I do not know what would appal them. If that is not " going it strong"; if that is not being on a colossal railway debauch for thirty years, I do not know what is. It seemed to make no difference during the last ten or fifteen years
how often you tried to call a halt; the carnival went on, and it was participated in just as boisterously by the party to which my hon. friend belongs and to which I myself once belonged. I opposed them on the Grand Trunk Pacific-Transcontinental policy however; I ran against the member of the Government in Western Canada who was pushing the thing through there; I have at least that to my credit.
I say that notwithstanding all that we have given, unless we stop now, we shall have to continue the carnival. Is it not about time that this condition came to an end? The Grand Trunk so say the company's officials themselves is at the end of its tether. Any one who studies the financial position of Canada knows that this country also will be practically at the end of its tether if it does not put a stop to this kind of thing. Here is the alternative: If you do not take over the Grand Trunk you will have to nurse the baby; you will have to continue pouring millions into the lap of that corporation to enable it to support the Grand Trunk Pacific and, probably, itself.
If we do not take the Grand Trunk, in order to make a success of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Intercolonial, we shall,have to build branch lines and terminals in Ontario, and that would involve a cost to the people of probably two hundred millions. And then what have we got? We have the Canadian Pacific, the Grand Trunk and our own system, all in competition. We cannot make a success of the state-owned system without the Grand Trunk. If we wipe it out, we wipe out its competition, and with a splendidly equipped System from the Atlantic to the Pacific we shall be able to effectively compete with the great Canadian Pacific Railway system. In no other way under the sun can we make a success of our national system of railways. That is the position which confronts the Government at the present time.
Hon. members argue strongly that the road should not be taken over, but they do not stop to think that if we do not take it over we shall have to support it. We have been supporting the railways, lame and otherwise, for the last thirty or forty years. Surely to Heaven we ought to have reached the end of the lane. It is such a reflection upon the judgment and the intelligence, not only of members of this House but of the people of the country as well, that I marvel that any sane person should continue this foolish policy an hour longer. It was inevitable that the time



should come when we would have to end it; and that time is the present.
I have made some reference to the policy of the so-called Liberal party in the old days when they launched this Transcontinental and Grand Trunk Pacific system. The then Minister of Finance, the present member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) who opposes this Bill, was the exponent and mouth-piece of the Government of that day. It was he who told us that the Transcontinental would cost the country only $13,000,000, whereas it 'has cost us over $200,000,000. I was looking over his speeches the. other day; it seemed to me that they were models of solemn absurdity and financial incompetence. I marvel that he takes the position that he now takes on this question, having regard to the vast blunder with which he was associated and which he helped drive through this Parliament and fasten upon the country. The only way in which the country can recoup itself for some of these losses is by taking over the Grand Trunk, co-ordinating it with our other publicly-owned lines and making it a thorough, competent, well-equipped system. When we do that we shall be able to make money out of it and probably get back some of the hundreds of millions that we have already spent.
Now, in what I am about to refer I should like to have the attention of the member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea). I hope that he will wake up and follow me closely, because I am coming to the declaration that he made last night-in which, no doubt, he was perfectly, sincere. I do not suppose the hon. gentleman knows that there is any country under the sun which has made a success of public ownership. I want to appeal especially to him because he is a hard-headed-shall I say hard-fisted'-business man. He knows how many beans make five; and, if I size him up correctly, I take it that if he thought that failure to acquire the Grand Trunk would add ten dollars to his taxes he would be in favour of taking it over and saving the ten dollars. I hope the hon. gentleman will appreciate the compliment.
In discussing the question of public versus private ownership, I want to make a prefatory remark, that the only thing to consider is not dollars and cents. It is not dividends that we must look at, especially, but service to the people. Does the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) appreciate that? It is not so much just whether we make five per cent or six per cent; we might make a little less, but if

we serve the people, that is the idea of public ownership-the subordination of dollars and cents to public service.

All these public
utilities that are in their nature natural monopolies, such as gas, water, light, telephones, telegraphs and railways, that enter into the service of the people, should belong to the people. Just let me tell the hon. member for Sherbrooke that people throughout the world have the idea of public ownership. Water, gas, light, telephones and telegraphs belong in the old land, as well as on this continent, very largely to the people themselves. It just occurs to me now that in Glasgow we have the greatest example of the success of public ownership that the world has ever witnessed. For the last twentydive years or more the whole street railway system and every other municipal service of that great city have been owned by the corporation of Glasgow. If my hon. friend has ever visited Glasgow, he will find that he can ride on a street car there for a penny and sometimes for a cent, and the revenue from that system is so vast that it has been almost entirely wiping out the taxes of the people of Glasgow for the last twenty or twenty-five years. That is one case. The conviction is being steadily forced upon the people, not only of Canada but of the world, that public ownership is in the general interest of the people, because it supplies them 'with service in preference to dividends, though it generally does return dividends. Let me suggest this to my hon. friend. He says that no success has ever been made of public ownership, and he challenges anybody in this House or out of it to produce any instance of its having proved a success. All the postal services, I presume, throughout the world, are under public ownership. Could a service be much better managed than even our own postal service which usually produces a revenue, notwithstanding the enormous disability, the 'Civil Service disability? In my judgment, the Civil Service should be taken by the heels and smashed against the wall; we are paying just double what we should pay for Civil Service at the present time, it could be cut in halves^ and its efficiency increased, arid yet we are going on and apouinting hundreds more to positions, mostly at big salaries.

own account. Naturally, just as the President of the Privy Council said last night, the interests immediately got busy and told us that the city was plunging into an enormous liability, just as the leader of the Opposition said last night with regard to this Grand Trunk business. The interests did their best to scare the people of Winnipeg from embarking upon this enterprise, but the people believed in public ownership; they thought they had a good thing in this Winnipeg River power and they appropriated sufficient money to develop it. Mark you they developed on the Winnipeg river up to 100,000 horse-power, and transmitted that power to the city. They spent $7,500,000, and at what rate do you suppose light has been distributed to the thousands of citizens of Winnipeg during. the last seven or eight years? Ten cents per kilowatt hour? No, three and-a-half cents per kilowatt hour. They cut the rate by more than two-thirds. The city of Winnipeg is supplied with light at the lowest rate,. I believe, on this continent, because of public ownership. The prices charged for power were reduced in the same proportion. Has public ownership in this case meant disaster for the city of Winnipeg? Not at all. During the last few years, in addition to paying interest on this $7,500,000 and providing a sinking fund, the city has been able to set aside $400,000 in profits, and the citizens have saved from one to two millions annually in the price of their light and power, because the competing privately-owmed company had to meet the new rate. There you have a magnificent example of the success of public ownership, and it will be that way all along the line wherever the principle is properly carried out.
I see it publicly stated that Sir Adam Beck's hydro-electric system has saved the people of Ontario fifty millions of dollars. The danger is in dishonest administration, and you cannot always safeguard yourself from the manipulations of scoundrels. But if you have public ownership and honest efficient administration it is bound to be a success. There is no reason why there should not be honest administration, and that brings me back again to the position of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. He says that we cannot get men who would serve the people as they would serve a corporation. I don't believe that is so. I give him credit for expressing what he believes to be true, but what reason under the sun is there why servants should not serve under a board of manage-

ment appointed by the Government just as faithfully and efficiently as under a board of management appointed by directors in old London? His position does not hold water.
While some friends on the other side of the House may vote against this proposal under the belief that they are doing a good turn to the country in striking at public ownership, I want to tell them in all solemnity that actually they are attempting to deal our national railways a deadly blow. Thank God, it will not be fatal to the principle of public ownership, which means so much for the interest of this country. Let them appeal to their old leader, Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, the man who created the Liberal party. Was he a private ownership man? No, he stood for public ownership. How the party has degenerated since his day! We have the remnant of the party here pleading for private ownership in a case where public ownership is the only possible remedy for the situation.
Opponents of public ownership very naturally point to failures and say: "Look at the Intercolonial." I have heard that said on every platform on which I have spoken on public ownership during the last twenty years. Let us examine the Intercolonial for a few minutes. As you especially know, Mr. Speaker, for you come from the Maritime Provinces, the Intercolonial was not built as a commercial enterprise. It was not expected1-and I want my hon. friends to mark this-that the country would make money out of it, but it was one of the terms of Confederation that the East should be connected by rail with the West. The Intercolonial was not built on a direct route, as a railway built for commercial purposes would have been, but followed a circuitous course around the coast line in order to serve this, that and the other community. Therefore, it could not be expected that it would be a commercial success. What has happened to the Intercolonial? As everybody knows, and especially the leader of the Opposition and hon. members from the Maritime Provinces, the road has been bled white for the last thirty or forty years. The cars used on the Intercolonial carry probably ten tons, but they would be set down as carrying only three or four tons, and while injury was done to the track the man who shipped freight over the Intercolonial got off with a very small payment. The curse of the Intercolonial has been political management and the foisting upon the line of thousands of incompetent political heelers and dependents, to the awful prejudice of the

enterprise. No wonder the ex-Minister oi Public Works (Mr. Carvell) and other hon. members from the Maritime Provinces look askance at public ownership, for they have seen what has happened. But the trouble has been with the management. The road has been a political railway to help out this, that, and the other politician. I venture to say that nothing of that sort will happen under the board that is administering the National Railways of Canada. We had an ebullition in connection with the Intercolonial from a politician not very long ago, when the then chief whip of the Conservative party threatened to resign because he w.as not given as great consideration from the Government in the matter of the Intercolonial railway patronage as he expected. The point I want to emphasize is this, and mark it, because it is worth while: The Intercolonial for thirty or forty years and until quite recently carried freight for less than one-third the amount charged by private-owned railways. Let that sink deep into the heart of my hon. friend, who I expect will vote for us before he is through. The country lost heavily, but Maritime Province residents got the benefit. I am satisfied that when the Intercolonial is amalgamated with the Grand Trunk system, which is required to link up the East with the West, we shall have a railway system that will pay.
Let me add that thousands and thousands of miles .of railway have been built in this country that never should have been built, much of it being simply >duplication. That is the result of this colossal railway blunder policy that has been carried on by both parties during the last twenty-five or thirty years. When we get the Grand Trunk incorporated into the public owned railway system, and have eliminated all waste mileage, swid let me add, all waste capital, we shall have a system that will pay interest on a reasonable capitalization, pay operating expenses, and give a valuable return to the people, if not in large dividends .at least in reduced rates. We have got the National Transcontinental, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Intercolonial, and the Canadian Northern now, but they are no good to us without the Grand Trunk system. They are like the cow of the leader of the Opposition that is not giving any milk.' We have to acquire the road that will complete our system, and when that is done my judgment is that we shall be able to give an excellent service to the people and make a profit into the bargain. But one thing will have to be done. Owing to the absurd system that has been followed by both parties in this country, and both parties are equally responsible, we have allowed railroad exploiters to persuade us to pour immense sums of money intq their maws in order that they might construct railway mileage, useless or otherwise, to enable them to make off with vast amounts in construction guarantees, etc. Because of that foolish policy-and both parties are equally to blame-we have hum dreds, if not thousands, of miles of unnecessary railway mileage in this country at the present time. That has to be eliminated. The capital cost has to be erased from the public ledger and the country has to. take the loss. If we acquire the Grand Trunk and co-ordinate it with our already publicly-owned system we shall have a complete system with which the country can compete efficiently with the Canadian Pacific and without which we cannot compete with that great corporation.
It is all very well for the leader of the Opposition to say: "Well, we already have one cow, let us see what that cow does before we buy another." Surely the hon. member knows that the cow is dry-dry as a whistle. It has never given a pint of milk ever since we had it and until we get another member of the bovine species and link them up we shall never have a productive and successful system. We might go on until the crack of doom with a big railway mileage in the West and a big railway mileage in the East, but without connections in the centre we cannot operate through trains, or make a success of the system. WTe can never make a success of this without this connection and unless we take over the Grand Trunk at the present time in order to make any success whatever of the thousands and thousands of miles we have, we shall have to build a system in central Canada to connect up with. We have either to take the Grand Trunk or build a connecting system in Ontario or Quebec. That would cost us from $100,000,000 to $200,000,000. That is the only way. You can not make a success of this cow unless you give her a companion. When we have acquired the Grand Trunk, and it is the only logical thing to do, we shall have a system in this country which I believe will be a paying institution and will be capable of effectively competing with the Canadian Pacific.
I -think it was the leader of the Opposition who spoke of the failure of public ownership in the United States; if it were not he it was some other member of the Opposition. In the United States, since the outbreak of the war, the railways have been
i

taken over and operated by the people. It is true they have not returned dividends to the people, but I will tell you what they did do; they helped to win the war. And if it had not been for the taking over of the railway system by the Government of the United States the United States could not have been as effective in France and Belgium as that country was at the period when its troops were there. The idea of profits was absolutely subordinated to winning the war. Before the Government of the United States undertook to control the railways there were 23,000 miles of American roads in the hands of receivers. That was under private ownership. It is not surprising that under public ownership during the war, when the service was subordinated to the carrying of troops they *did not make a very great success of the *operation. In addition, however, there is far too much- water in the stocks of the American roads to make a success. Great Britain took over and operated its railways. I read recently in a white-book issued by the Government that during the operation of the roads by the Government they earned a profit of $81,000,000.
With regard to the Bill under consideration and which provides for the taking over of the Grand Trunk, I may say that the Grand Trunk owes the Government $90,000,000 under the Grand Trunk Pacific contract. I a,m informed, as I said at the outset, that when the agreement for arbitration comes to be made the interest of the people will be guarded. I am informed that no appreciation of Grand Trunk stock in the old land since it was known that the Government was negotiating for its purchase will be recognized. I am informed that the arbitrators will perfectly guard the interest of the public. If that is true I do not see that there is going to be any very great danger in taking over the road. Of the $115,000,000 of common stock of the Grand Trunk, I am told that no more than $15,000,000 actually represents money put into the railway. A lot of this money has been wasted. Of course, the stock sold very much below par and the money has been wasted. I do not think we have very much to fear in connection with taking over the line. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) says that he is not opposed to public ownership but that the greatest and best public men of Canada are. I think those are his words.
