speechtext:
Well, I have not got the ear of the Government. I have not got that assurance from them, and I am unable to give my hon. friend that assurance.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, and I have taken up much longer time than I had intended, a word or two in conclusion. We are faced in this matter with the alternative of pouring millions and millions of dollars into the hands of the corporation unless we take a radical step, such as is proposed at this time, and take over this railway. Then we shall have a publicly-owned railway system which, will serve the whole country, and, I believe, serve it efficiently.
I am not of the view that the Canadian Pacific railway should be taken over. It is a magnificent railway system efficiently managed and pays well and every body wishes it well. No wonder it pays well in view, as I have shown the House, of the vast amount of money the country has given to it. I would have the Canadian Pacific railway continue as a competing road, and I think that if it remains so the public will be better served than if it becomes incorporated in our national railway system.
When we get this Grand Trunk Railway system incorporated in our own national system, as I believe we shall in a very short time, the next thing to do will be for this Parliament to eliminate all waste mileage from the public owned system, and write the cost off the ledger. Then we ought to charge rates sufficient to pay in-

terest on the reasonable cost, and only the reasonable cost, of the road, and maintenance and upkeep. If we start off with a fair capitalization we ought soon to be in a position to make the system pay as an enormous saving can he at once effected in the elimination of hundreds if not thousands of officials and offices which are now duplicated. But without a fair capitalization it is impossible, in my judgment, to make a success of our venture. The point is very important. Take the Grand Trunk road, its capitalization although constructed when material and labour were absurdly cheap has climbed to the enormous figure of $127,000 a mile. The capitalization of the Canadian Pacific, which was built under pretty favourable auspices, is $69,000 a mile, the Canadian Northern still lower $54,000 a mile, and the Grand Trunk Pacific which was built under very bad auspices, as indicated by the report showing $40,000,000 of extravagance and graft, cost $98,000 a mile. $127,000 a mile is an enormous capitalization, for it must be remembered that the Grand Trunk was built in the early days, and I do not see how it could have cost that large sum. But I suppose there were railway exploiters and manipulators, and they probably sold railroads on political bases to the Grand Trunk just as readily in those days as in more modern times, which probably largely accounts for the enormous capitalization. The Manitoba Railway system which the Northern Pacific built some twenty years ago only cost $9,000 a mile. Compare with that the capitalization of the Grand Trunk at $127,000 a mile! Of course, that includes equipment. But the difference is out of all proportion. And the Canadian Pacific even at $68,000 a mile is much too high. However, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company added to their capital. They issued tens of thousands of dollars worth of capital stock. They distributed the original first issue of stock among themselves at 25 cents on tlhe dollar, set the proceeds aside and paid themselves interest at 6 per cent, and in four years recouped themselves every farthing they paid for it, and they owned the stock into the bargain. That is the way these transactions have been carried out. The city of Winnipeg built a railroad 100 miles in length out to Shoal lake, along the waterworks aqueduct, on the Lake of the Woods, and from the figures I have obtained the cost of construction and equipment - of course, the equipment is not great- was but $12,000 a mile-all constructed within the last five years. If we are to make a
success of our publicly owned system, it is very important that we reduce the capitalization to the figure it would take to reproduce the system, and then let us pay interest on that reasonable capitalization, which will enable us to give the people rates very much less than are being charged at the present time.
I think that politics can be kept out of the management of this publicly owned system, Mr. Speaker. I have yet to learn of any political interference since the Intercolonial railway and the Canadian Northern railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific passed into the hands of the board at present managing them-at least no complaints have reached me-and I believe it is the duty, as I am advised it is the resolute intention, of this Government to keep the system absolutely free from politics. If it does, I have no doubt that we can operate it successfully.
Last session I took the view that it would be unfortunate if we had to take over this Grand Trunk system under arbitration owing to our distressing ten million experience with the wretched Canadian Northern railway stock, but there seems no help for it. I am told that the difficulties of allowing the system to pass into the hands of a receiver and then acquiring it would be insurmountable, because so much of the system is in the United States. I am told that event the plan of purchasing or guaranteeing to pay a certain return on the bonds and stocks would not do because we cannot acquire control. I hope when the time comes to appoint arbitrators we shall get a good business board. God protect us from too many legal quibblers on the board. I do not think we ought to have lawyers-we might have one legal gentleman. But if we have a business arbitration, and the arbitration agreement which I rely upon is of the right character, I cannot help thinking that the country does not take much risk even in going into arbitration. The difficulty, however, is that for two years the Government has been endeavouring to acquire the road by purchase. We said that we would guarantee so much interest on the bonds and debentures, but the Grand Trunk people would not accept our offer, and nearly two years ago the Government proposed arbitration. Arbitration seems to be the reasonable thing under the circumstances. If you and I, Mr. Speaker, cannot agree upon a certain point, I would think you would have a right to feel very much offended if I declined to agree to submit our difference to

a third, party. Surely we can get justice from arbitration, providing it is of the right character. If we have business arbitrators I should think they would at least do justice to the people of Canada. I would not like to see three judges appointed. I think the arbitration board should be composed of two business men, with perhaps a judge as a third man to look into the legal aspect of the case.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I must apologize for having taken up so much of the time of the House, but this is a great subject and perhaps none of greater economic importance has come before this House in the last twenty-five years. The issue means a great deal to this country. I do not know whether the arbitration agreement will foe submitted to the House, but when we are in Committee on the resolution I suppose we shall have every opportunity for further discussion. I want to say in conclusion that 1 find difficulty in understanding the Liberal party-or the remains of the Liberal party- offering opposition to public ownership in view of the position which the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, practically the creator of the party, took on this very question. It must be a compelling spectacle to the interested historian and to every reflective citizen to see the descendants of the old Conservative guard allied with the progressive elements of the old Liberal party in carrying out the most progressive legislation which this country has ever witnessed, whilst the apparently all too willing, even if unconscious, remnants of the once proud and virile party created by Brown and MacKenzie appear in this House as the agents or servants of arrogant and malign interests to try to block this important legislation.

It seems to me that every one who knows Sir Henry Drayton, who made this report, knows what a careful man he is in making statements, knqws also the advantages that he has had from having presided over the Board of Railway Commissioners, and when he and Mr. Acworth, the great English authority who was associated with him, made that statement, we have a right to assume it is correct.
I wish now to draw the attention of hon. members to a statement made by Mr. A. H. Smith, President of the New York Central Railway Company and Chairman of this Royal Commission. He stated, concerning what we call the Drayton-Acworth report, that the plan proposed by Sir Henry Drayton and Mr. Acworth of taking over the railway would add about $1,000,000,000 to the debt of Canada. The interest on this, he says, would be about $40,000,000. He also points out that the fundamental defect of their plan is in placing the Government in the railroad business in which they would be operating railways not only in Canada but in the United States where they would be subject to both Federal and State regulations. That will be found at page ci. Mr. iSmith as we know is a man of great experience. He is the head of one of the greatest railway systems of the United States. He and Sir Henry Drayton went over every part of this system and made a careful personal examination. Mr. Acworth came later and did not go over the system.
There you have the opinion of a railway expert with a thorough knowledge of United States conditions, and in his opinion the amount required would be $1,000,000,000. He further points out the fundamental defect of a plan under which the Government of Canada would endeavour to operate a system of railways with such a large mileage in the United States where they would be subject to Federal and State legislation. Mr. Smith proposes, at page cii, a plan or scheme by which this operation could be carried on. As I remember it, without troubling the House by reading the report, briefly it was that the Government should get the Canadian Northern and Grand Trunk Pacific in the West, that they should make a traffic arrangement with the Grand Trunk in the East and that with the Grand Trunk they should operate these systems. Then we have an alternative plan proposed at page civ. It is to form a private company and to give the company an opeiating lease to induce private enterprise to undertake the management with a profit sharing plan which would give the public a share in the profits. You will of course under-
stand that Mr. Smith was against government ownership. His alternative scheme was to get a private company to take over the properties. They would be under the control and subject to the regulations and orders of the Railway Commission; they would be induced, of course, by the agreement that would be made, to embark capital in this enterprise, and any profits made would be shared with the Government. That seemed to me to be a practical scheme, a good scheme, and one that I think it would have been wise for Canada to adopt -it would have been wise for this country to take Mr. Smith's advice on that point.
I will not detain the House with any further figures in connection with these enormous obligations, and interest obligations, that we will have to assume on taking over this road. The figures are so big that a person can hardly grasp them. We are accustomed now to speaking about millions, and then we get up to billions, and we toss these figures about as if they were merely dollars. Really, Mr. Speaker, it is difficult for a man to grasp or to take account of the enormous sums of money which we have expended, and which we will have to raise in the future to meet further obligations.

That means that -for a great number of years past the Grand Trunk Railway Company have practically been bankrupt. If that company is not bankrupt, if they can go on as they have been going on without assistance or help, what is the necessity for our stepping in and grabbing that road from the shareholders'-paying them back part of their stock investments and carrying on the railway as a government concern? Further than that, we know that the reason

the Canadian Northern was not successful was its unlawful ambition, so to speak, to parallel other lines of railway in order to get a terminus on the Pacific coast. And it is the same with the Grand Trunk Pacific; they have made enormous expenditures in order to be able to say that they went to the Pacific coast. That is also the reason why we are assuming these great obligations at the present time-simply to say that we have got a road from the Atlantic to the Pacific owned by the Government of Canada. What I am endeavouring to show now is Canada's financial position-the position in which we stand at the present time. I am satisfied, Mr. Speaker, and I want to satisfy the House, that our financial position is not such as will permit us at the present time to undertake these great obligations. For the purpose of illustrating my point, let me endeavour to strike a trial balance. Canada started business in 1867 with a gross debt of ninety-three millions and an interest liability of $4,500,000. In 1914 our debt had grown to $544,000,000; and our present debt, I believe, to be about $2,000,000,000 in round figures. There is another matter we require to look at. We have become a borrowing country. Canada must borrow money, enormous sums of money, to carry on. We have already borrowed great amounts, but we have to borrow more. We shall have to negotiate another loan after the present one -perhaps one or two more after that.
What is our financial position? Besides the great debt of about $2,000,000,000 that we owe at the present time our various provinces owe very large sums of money. I have here a statement showing the indebtedness of all the different provinces, and without giving the details I may state that the gross amount is $264,706,000. And you must remember that some of these are short-term obligations. You must likewise bear in mind that the provinces must also go into the market to borrow money. You must further recollect that we have got to raise in Canada
the money that requires to be borrowed now, because we have been told by the late Minister of Finance that we practically cannot borrow it outside; the only amount that we could borrow in the United States would be about $75,000,000, and on the last loan of that amount we had to pay a very stiff rate of interest. We cannot assume that we can borrow in the United States more than $100,000,000, therefore, we must take a survey of the financial position of this Dominion and the financial position of the several provinces. Let me go a step further and give you a statement of the municipal indebtedness, because that is a matter that must be taken into consideration. You have to go to our great cities and to our prosperous counties in order to get money from our own people. The municipalities will have to borrow money in the future; they have to pay interest on the money they have already borrowed; and they must renew these loans, which means more money to be borrowed. It is difficult to arrive at the municipal indebtedness, but I find that taking 62 cities and towns in Canada the total bonded indebtedness amounts to $456,000,000. The population of these cities and towns amounts to 2,598,000, making an indebtedness per head of $210.17. Now if these cities and towns are fairly representative of the whole of Canada, the latter figure would yield a key 'to the situation. The total population of Canada residing in urban communities of over 500 inhabitants is 3,281,000, and therefore the total municipal indebtedness for the Dominion, based on the figures I have already given, $210.17 per head, would amount to $689,500,000. That, of course, is an estimate. If any gentleman would like to have my authority for these figures I shall be very glad to furnish it, but I am quite positive the statement is absolutely correct. Now then, let us sum up: Canada's net debt at the present time is about two billions. The debts of the provinces amount to $264,500,000; and the municipal indebtedness $689,500,000; or a total for Canada of $2,954,000,000, almost $3,000,000,000.
But in addition to this we have to look after our other liabilities. Here is a statement made by Mr. Fred. Field of the Monetary Times, in regard to our external liabilities:
British capital invested' in Canada $1,878,900,000; United States capital invested in Canada $1,272,850,000 ; estimated Canadian flotations in London upon to 1918, over $937,000,000 ; or total liabilities of about $4,089,750,000.

Then there is our indebtedness to investors in France and Holland, which he estimates at about $5,000,000. These figures, of course, it may be said, have no bearing on the matter. But they have this bearing, and a very important one, too, that financial people when lending money to a country naturally want to know what are the liabilities of that country, and they would look not only at our national, but also at our provincial and municipal debts, because they know that in order to redeem these loans we have to go to our own people to raise the money.	.
In his Budget speech of June last Sir Thomas White gave us the financial condition of the Dominion. He stated:
This is a war year and it was necessary also to add the estimated expenditure which has been and will be incurred on account of demobilization. This will aggregate the large sum of $300,000,000, including $92,000,000 for war gratuity. The entire estimated expenditure, therefore, of the year on ordinary account, capital account and for demobilization will reach the large total of $620,000,000.
And he gives the items making up our revenue for the year, which he fixes at $280,000,000. Then he proceeds:
While from the statement which I have just made it will appear from our total estimated expenditure, ordinary and capital accounts, and for demobilization, will amount to $620,000,000, our estimated revenue on the present basis will reach only $280,000,000. Putting it another way, our revenue would enable us to pay only our ordinary expenditure and leave a small amount to be applied to other purposes.
Sir Thomas White also stated that:
This year the I>ominion Government mU3t find not only its ordinary expenditure of $270,000,000, for which its revenue will barely suffice (in fact I doubt if it will meet the ordinary expenditure) but also the capital expenditure of $50,000,000. In addition to that, large expenditures in government railway systems, ship building programme and expensive credits which we have been obliged to give to Great Britain and other countries. The amounts involved are exceedingly large. Outside of England, about $106,.(HM),000>
of credits have been issued, viz.: to Belgium Prance, Italy, Rou-mania and Greece.
Then he takes up the question of how we are to raise this money. He stated that our ordinary revenue is not quite sufficient to meet our ordinary expenditure. As to additional revenue from taxation, he states that the main source of our revenue is our customs, our inland revenue, our income tax and our business profits war tax. As regards our income tax, in his opinion, it cannot be made any higher. It is now as high as the United States' income tax. Then he points out the fact

that as regards income tax there is a provincial income tax in some of the provinces, a municipal income tax, and the federal income tax, and he gives as an example the province of British Columbia, where they have three sets of taxes imposed on income; and in Nova Scotia they have two. He also stated that our business profits war tax would be renewed. In view of the circumstances Sir Thomas White said he did not see any escape from our floating another loan. Out of the loan we were then making, he stated, $300,000,000 was due to the banks, and that they might agree to $72,000,000 of that amount standing over for another year, but that that would mean we would have to make another loan at least next fall.
If we are taxed to the limit now, what is left to us? Mr. R. W. Breadner, Commissioner of Taxation, and Sir Thomas White are of the opinion that practically the only further tax that can be levied is a tax upon land-and the farmers of this country may as well know the position we are coming to. Such a tax will mean that every farm will have to pay taxation according to a valuation. As pointed out by Mr. Breadner, it is a difficult tax to collect, because, it requires such a large number of people to make the valuation and collection. I have here also the statement of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) with regard to the financial condition of the country, but I shall not read it; it is in line with that which was made by the ex-Minister [DOT]of Finance (Sir Thomas White).
Now, to sum up, this is the way the case presents itself to me. We have great resources, and in order to develop those resources, we want capital. If we impose taxes which are too severe we shall prevent the investment here of the capital which is necessary to the development of our resources. Moreover, we have to raise large sums of money by way of loans, without taking into consideration at all any liability imposed upon us in respect to the Grand Trunk. There may be another large loan next year; shall we he able to raise that money in Canada? In view of these circumstances, this country ought to go slowly; in the words of the railway watchword, we must "stop, look, listen." There is no necessity for our rushing in and taking over the Grand Trunk at this time. The bugaboo is put before us :hat if we do not take it over the Canadian Pacific will take it. But in order to take over the Grand Trunk the Canadian Pacific must come to this Parliament for the

necessary legislative authority, and in that legislative authority we can impose whatever -restrictions we think proper. But it is idle to -think that the matter will be considered at all by the Canadian Pacific at this time. Besides, look at the obligations of the Grand Trunk in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Do you think that any private company would take over the Grand Trunk with all those enormous obligations standing against it? The Government, as mortgagee, have the most absolute control over the Grand Trunk. They need not take it over; they can take it over two or three years hence just a-s well as they can do it now, and in the meantime they can go ahead and attend to the business that is in hand-that of developing and managing the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific, the latter being in the hands of the Government as receiver.
The Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) says that the management of this road, should it be taken over, will be kept entirely out of politics; that no political influence	will be exerted	in connection with it in any shape or form. Well, who appoints the manager and directors?	The	Governor in Council.
Who fixes their salaries? The Governor in Council, I suppose. Who has to supply the money -for the deficits? The country, through the Government; we must supply the money. Do you mean to say that the Government are not going to exercise any control over the expenditure or the management of that road? If the Government wanted anything done, would the manager dare to refuse to carry out instructions? That reminds me of an old s-to-ry. Commodore Vanderbilt had bought some new cars for the New York Central. He called in his head painter -and said: " Now, Tom, you are absolute in your own department;
I would not think of interfering in any way. 1 want these -cars painted; I don't care a darn What colour you paint -them as long as you paint them red." It will be -something the same with the instructions that will go out -from the minister to the manager of the Government railway system: " You can do as you please-if you do so-and-so and so-and-so.''
I may add that throughout the country a spirit of distrust prevails with respect to the -management of the Government railway system. I have nothing to say against Mr. Hanna, the general manager; he seems to be a very capable man. But for ye-ars be a-cted for the Canadian Northern as the servant of Mackenzie and Mann, and nat-79
ur-ally one would think -that Sir William Mackenzie could exercise a great deal of influence over our general manager if he wanted to. Mr. Hanna and Mr. Mitchell will be practically in control of our great rail-way system. Of course, if they do not carry -out their work efficiently the Government can, and (probably will, make a change. But it is a fact that the country has not absolute confidence in t'he men who are managing our national railways, and this attitude is due to the -manner in which these men were educated in railway work by Mackenzie and Mann and to the fact that certain men- interested in railway matters are now their bosom friends. To these men they would naturally go f-or advice, and as I say these men could, if they wished, exercise some influence over them.
My other objection to the taking over of this road is based on my opposition to government ownership. For many years I have been opposed to public ownership. In 1891 when my partner and I bought the Daily Telegraph we published a number of articles against government ownership. In 1903-04 when the matter of the Grand Trunk Pacific was put before the country I came out on the hustings against government ownership and in favour of private control. I believe in government control through the Railway Commission,-and if that body did not have sufficient powers, I was in favour of giving full and ample power to them. I have always been strong and consistent in my opposition to government ownership.
Just in that connection, some one said to me during the recess for dinner: " It is all very well for you to oppose this thing; you are solicitor for the Canadian Pacific." Well, I am like a great many other professional gentlemen in this House who have taken retainers from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I am glad to say that never at any time during which I have acted for the Canadian Pacific have they attempted in any way to influence my action on the occasion of an election. I will give you an example. On the occasion of the reciprocity campaign I was a candidate. I had then some heavy retainers from the Canadian Pacific in connection with large matters of business. Sir William Van Horne came to my county and spoke against me. But he did not attempt to influence me, and his attitude made no difference whatever so far as their having further dealings with me was concerned. Hon. members know whether the Canadian Pacific have been sympathetic with the Liberals or with the Conservatives during the



last number of years. Until the last election I had been a strong) fighting Liberal, but during all the time that I was active and aggressive as a Liberal the Canadian Pacific Railway Company did not attempt to influence my vote in any way or to do anything which would affect my position in politics.
I do not believe that the Canadian Pacific would in any way interfere with the solicitors who act in their interests. There are /horn, members sitting on your right, Sir, who can back -me up in that statement. From time to time, statements have been made that the Canadian Pacific conducts lobbies. I am not in the secrets of the Canadian Pacific, but I do not know personally of any such lobby having been conducted in this House, and I think I can fairly make the statement that no hon. member can say that he has ever been approached by any Canadian Pacific official endeavouring to influence him in this matter. As regards public ownership, the Canadian Pacific may have a different opinion from the one I hold; I do not think they hold such strong views in the matter as I do. For example, this is a statement given out to the press a short time ago by Mr. Beatty, President of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company:
The desire of every one is that Canada to-day should have a railway system, or systems, so administered that the hest service to the public will he obtained at the lowest rates consistent with fair wages, both for labour and capital. 1 say fair wages because without them efficiency, loyalty and enterprise cannot be obtained, and without these things the quality of work which ensures efficient operation and low rates cannot be secured..
I am sure that every one will agree with that statement.
The question therefore is: Will government ownership bring about this result? the question sounds simple but is in reality complex. Theoretically much may be said in favour of government ownership. Will those theories stand the test of practice? If those theories prove a failure initially but correct themselves, in course of time, as their exponents may urge, how long a time can the Canadian people afford to pay the losses on a demoralised railway service?
That seems a fair and common sense statement. He does not come out in favour of government ownership, but he says: There is what is required; will government ownership bring about this result? If it does not, it means on the other hand that tbe service will be demoralized. Then he says:
Do they wish to launch out on the experiment now. or wait until our near neighbours, the United States, have worked out their ex-

perlment a little more satisfactorily? The cost of our own experiment could not fail to he great, a cost certain to be collected, directly or indirectly, from the pockets of the Canadian people. Railway men have an admirable slogan which I feel inclined to commend to the attention of the people of Canada at this moment, namely, "Stop, look, listen."
That seems to be a fair, strong and able statement. Mr. Beatty goes on to give his own views:
X have my own views on public ownership of railways, but they are not unalterable. I am undoubtedly prejudiced by association with one company. That company has slowly developed to a point of efficiency and successful operation. Looking back over that history one is amazed at the importance of the part played by men whose enterprise, resourcefulness and tenacity of purpose could not, I think, have been stimulated and given rein in any civil service. It has taken more than thirty odd years to make the Canadian Pacific railway as efficient as it is to-day. It was not easy. The consciousness that it is so easily shattered is largely responsible for the constant and intense ambition on the part of officers and men to maintain, and even improve on, the tradition.
This much may, it seems to me, be said with confidence now, namely, that we do not know enough that is encouraging about government operation of large railway systems to justify any furl her excursions into that field at this time.
This man of great experience, head of one of the great railway systems, without giving a statement in favour of government ownership, but stating the facts as he' has done fairly and fully, says that we do not know enough yet about the operation of large railway systems to justify any further excursions into that field now, that is, the field of government ownership.
To argue from the experience of old countries where civil service obtains a much better share of the ambitious young men than in Canada, or to argue from the alleged success of comparatively local affairs, or government organizations dominated by exceptional personalities, is unfair-not to the railways, but to the country which has so much at stake in this issue. We can well afford to wait, to study dispassionately our own situation, and the experiment of the United States, before committing our country to serious changes in policy. The solution finally adopted in the United States will be of inestimable value to Canada, meantime too, the experience which Canada will now have of the present newly organized government system will demonstrate many things. It will indicate very largely the general nature of thfe results we may hope to secure from an extension of the system. . . .
I invite hon. members to consider carefully this statement made by the President of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.

I have a great respect for my hon. friend's judgment, and I would, therefore, like to ask him a question. Assuming that the Grand Trunk is unable to carry on without further assistance from this Government, and the other fact that this Government owns and controls the Intercolonial, the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental, what alternative would the hon. member suggest to the Government's proposition?
Mr. H. H. MoLEAN:	It would be very
difficult for me, with no knowledge of railway operations, with the very limited experience that I have had, to outline, just on the call of the minute, a general scheme for the management of a great
9 p.m. railway system. That is for the Government themselves to consider, but I brought before the House the opinion of the President of the New York Central, the Chairman of this Railway Commission, a man of vast experience and knowledge, and he condemns utterly government operation of Canadian railway systems for the reasons that he gives in his report, and he proposes a private company to be formed under such restrictions and in such a manner as will safeguard the interest of the country and ensure such efficient operation as will induce capital to go into that company. You would have all the safeguards of a Railway Commission and other safeguards surrounding it and, as he says, the profits are to be divided. Thus we would have private operation, private ambition, and the country would get the service and would have the profits divided. That is one proposal made by Mr. Smith.
I am very glad to say that I shall be through very soon. When I got up to make an address, -T thought it would take me only a few minutes. I felt I had to give the reasons why I was voting against the Rill, and I endeavoured to boil down my reasons and make them as short as possible.
To sum up. I am against Government ownership. I have been for a number of years in favour of private ownership and Government control. This we have through the Railway Commission. Their control has been efficient and effectual, and their decisions have commanded the respect of all railway men. It is impossible for me in the limited time at any disposal to go 79*
fully into the arguments against public ownership. Books and pamphlets by the hundred have been issued on public ownership, pro and con. My principal grounds of objection are: First, the inability of state-owned roads to earn sufficient money to pay interest on the capital invested. Second, the interjection of politics into the service to the detriment of discipline, and at heavy cost to the Government. Third, the failure of the Government to operate the railways strictly as a business proposition. Fourth, the service, both passenger and freight, becomes worse. Fifth, it is a step towards socialism.
I do not want to argue these grounds in detail. As I have said, authorities pro and con have issued pamphlets on the subject by the hundreds. The authorities I have are Mr. Acworth, one of the members of the Drayton-Acworth Commission, who in his book makes a strong statement against Government ownership, and Ralgrave, the great authority on political economy, who also makes a strong statement against it. I will not take up the time of the House to read extracts, but will only say that these*are two great authorities. Of course, I know authorities sometimes differ, just as in law cases; one side will bring forward what seems conclusive authority, to he followed by equally conclusive authority from the other side, and it is for the judge to decide. In this case it is for the House of Commons to decide, and on their decision we must rely.
The hon. memlber for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) said this afternoon that the operation of railways in Great Britain under Government ownership had been a great success. My hon. friend must have been misinformed. I have a statement here showing that the railways of Great Britain before being taken over by the Government were on a 4 per cent earning basis, and the Government guaranteed these earnings when they took over the roads. Under Government management the estimated annual deficit is about $440,000,000, or as Sir Eric Geddeis said, about $1,250,000 a day. The British Government must continue to operate these railways for two years more and pay rental to the owners. In the United States the roads were taken over by the Government after the war had been on for a long time, during which time all the great trunk systems there had been showing a fair profit. When the Government took over the roads they guaranteed to the shareholders the average net earnings for the three years prior to the war, and if

no profit was made the shareholders ,re-ceived no dividends. What was the result? Mr. A. B. Cummings, Chairman of the Committee of Interstate 'Commerce of the United Slates Senate, on August 5, 1919, said fpage 3W0, Congressional Record):
We lost 240 million last year, and we lost ri the four or five months of this year 260 million; and we are now losing at the rate of 39 million per month.	[DOT]
That has 'been the experience of Great Britain and the United States. True it may be said that these are war times, when the cost of labour and materials is abnormally high, Then why does not the Government stop, look, and listen, and wait for two or three years until conditions become more normal? Why rush in at this time and incur the enormous charges that will have to be borne?
Now let us see what has been done under private ownership. The Canadian Pacific railway under private ownership and private control has also had to pass through the war period, and was subject to the same conditions in regard to high cost of material and everything else as the government-controlled roads, but the Canadian Pacific has been able to pay full dividends to their shareholders and put by a handsome surplus, besides contributing large sums for war purposes. They were able to assist Great Britain's financing in the United States by putting up their valuable securities. Contrast that with the results obtained under Government ownership.
I regret I have taken up so much time. Not being a speaker, I thought it would not take long to make my statement, but it takes a very much longer time than an inexperienced speaker would expect. I wish to draw the attention of the Minister of Railways to a matter in which the people of St. John are vitally interested. Mr. J. D. Reid:	So far as I am concerned,

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to follow the argument of the hon. member from Royal (Mr. McLean) at any great length, but I would direct the attention of the House to the fact that he has just now stated that he is opposed to Government ownership. He has been opposed to Government ownership since 1891. He was opposed to it in 1903 and 1904, and he assisted the Government of that day in bringing about the legislation whereby the Grand Trunk Pacific was brought into being, which is now saddled on this Government and upon the bonds of which they are now compelled to pay the interest. The hon. gentleman was a supporter of the Government that carried out that proposition.
He talks about the financial affairs of this country. Had it not been for the enormous sums of money that were spent on the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental, it would be an easy matter for us to finance the affairs of Canada at the present time. The hon. member for Royal calls attention to the fact that the Grand Trunk agreement of

1904 had a clause in it by which the company were compelled to route certain freight to St. John and Halifax. If the shipper in Canada wished to have his freight routed to St. John and Halifax they were compelled to ship it that way. But there was no other arrangement whereby they were compelled to ship it in that way if not so directed toy the shipper.
He calls attention to the fact that the Government of this country are likely to ship a great deal of freight to Portland. Let me inform him that the Grand Trunk Railway Company, with their double track from Niagara Falls to Chicago, handle on that line enormous quantities of freight gathered in the latter city, brought on through Toronto down to Montreal and shipped to Portland. Why? Because the shipper in the United States definitely and distinctly asks that these goods he shipped through Canada to Portland. The Grand xrumk Railway Company have been able to acquire hundreds of thousands of dollars every year on the freight that is shipped in that way, and it would be folly for this Government, or any other body of men who migni, take over this railway, to attempt to say to the people of the United States: " We will not carry your freight through Canada and on to Portland for shipment to Europe." Let me tell the hon. gentleman- and I feel confident the Minister of Railways will concur in the statement-that it is not the intention of the Government to ship any freight by way of Portland, unless a shipper in Canada asks that it shall be so shipped, and I will give him the reason for this statement. The hon. gentleman knows full well that within the last year we have undertaken a shipping policy, we have undertaken to construct fifty-two vessels in Canada. To w'hat use are these vessels- to be put? They are to be placed at our ports, Halifax, St. John, Quebec and Montreal for the purpose of carrying the products- of thif country to the markets of the world. But does not the hon. gentleman realize that, especially when the winter months come, the Canadian Government will see to it that every pound of freight they can get is shipped over the National railway to the ports of -St. John and Halifax? It would be folly to expect that this Government, or any commission appointed by them, would dare to route their freight or passengers, if they possibly could do otherwise, via Portland instead of via St. John, Halifax, and our other ports. The hon. gentleman has not offered any alternative for the proposition

which he condemns; he says he has no alternative to propose. In that -case, why argue this question? The Government has got to deal with the situation. We cannot possibly wait for one or two years, as the hon. gentleman has suggested. We have a disorganized, disconnected and disjointed government railway system, and the sooner we get that system rounded up, organized and put in -proper condition the better it will be for the public. Instead *of waiting for months and years we cannot, in my opinion, act too quickly in this matter. I take that position believing and knowing that is is in the best interests of our people to take over the Grand Trunk, round up our great national system, and place it in a position where it will he able to compete with the Canadian Pacific. I have heard men say within the last few days that this bargain is going to interfere with the Government loan which is now being asked for. Some men have even gone so far as to make this statement-I heard of one man that went to another who was likely to subscribe for a bond and said to him: Why the money you are going to put into that bond will be taken and put into this Grand Trunk Railway .system. It is not the intention of the Government to use one dollar, that they collect from the people in connection with this loan, or to use it in any way towards the development of this railway system. All the Government are seeking is to have this enabling Act passed whereby they will be able to bring about a definite agreement with the .stockholders of the Grand Trunk in England.
Now let us look at another point or two which the hon-. gentleman has raised. It is not altogether a question of public ownership. The present legislation is rendered necessary by reason of the failure of private ownership. The hon. gentleman knows right well that in the year 1903-4 the Grand Trunk entered into a definite arrangement to build the Grand Trunk Pacific. It is true that an enormous sum of money has been put into the latter railway and taken from the public treasury for that purpose, and it is also true that the Grand Trunk have advanced a considerable sum towards its construction. But we are to-day in this position: Ther Grand Trunk threw up their responsibilities as regards the Grand Trunk Pacific and practically forced this Government to take over that portion of their system. Does the hon. gentleman want us -simply to take

over the Grand Trunk Pacific and not the Grand Trunk? Does he want us to take over the lean end of the proposition, the end that cannot pay for many years to come, and allow the Grand Trunk which is the profitable end, that has always paid the interest on Its bonds, to continue in opposition to the government-owned railway? If the hon. gentleman will go to Western Ontario to-day, he will find that freight is being routed by way of Chicago to the western provinces of Canada instead of being routed by North Bay and on through to Winnipeg over the National Transcontinental. Why? Because this Government has been compelled to take over the Grand Trunk Pacific and the thousand miles of line between North Bay and Winnipeg is in the hands of the receiver. The Grand Trunk Railway Company can therefore make more money out of the long haul through Chicago, and over their own line In the United States to Winnipeg, than they would make if they were compelled to bring that freight round by North Bay. But when the Canadian Government system is re-organized and rounded up, you can depend upon it the passengers and freight from the western portion of the province of Ontario will foe sent by North Bay, and will help to develop this National Transcontinental system and help to make it a paying proposition. My reason for taking an active interest in this - debate is because I feel particularly anxious about the interest of the western Ontario peninsula. If you run a line through the centre of the city of Toronto from lake Ontario north to the Georgian bay, west of that line, there are 1,500,000 Canadians, represented by 45 members in this House, this is the most thickly peopled area in any portion of Canada. More factories are located in this district than in all the rest of Canada put together. This district has an assessed value of $1,-
100,000,000, yet not one mile of the Canadian Northern, of the Transcontinental, of the Grand Trunk Pacific, of the Intercolonial-not one mile of the government-owned railways to-day enters this great district. These people have as good a right to be served by our national system of railways as the people of any 'other district. Do you want to build lines to parallel the Grand Trunk and make it worthless? For in that district you find the Grand Trunk running into every city, town and village; their double track running through to Chicago and with connections from Niagara Falls on to New York, a double track runs from the city of London to the city of Windsor; another double track runs from the city of Hamilton to the city of Toronto; you find a single track runs along the northern shore of lake Erie; another single track runs from Toronto through St. Mary's and Stratford to Sarnia, other tracks run north and south. The whole country is served and served well by the Grand Trunk; when that system is connected up with our national railways it will become a mighty power in assisting the management of our national railway system in bringing about a successful operation of all lines.
This system is largely located in western Ontario and in the province of Quebec and in the eastern provinces. The Canadian Northern runs from Quebec to Montreal through our north country to Winnipeg, and there they commence a splendid transportation system of 6,500 miles covering the very best territory in the Northwest. But this end of the line is practically without branches or feeders. The Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental are in worse position, because the Transcontinental starts at Moncton, and runs through Quebec and our north country to Winnipeg, where it connects with the Grand Trunk Pacific, running to Edmonton and on to Prince Rupert-one long band of steel practically across the continent, with very few feeders. How can we expect, unless we link up this other system with it, that we can poSsibly make our national system a. paying proposition? Look at the position the Intercolonial railway has been in for many years, coming up from the Atlantic coast to Quebec and Montreal, without a terminal in Montreal and with very few feeders. Even the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) within the last few weeks has been urging the Minister of Railways to build branches in the eastern provinces connecting them with the Intercolonial railway. The Intercolonial railway would be a power in this country today if in 1903 and 1904 hon. gentlemen opposite supported the proposition of Government ownership of a railroad connecting with the Intercolonial and running through to the West. We would then have had a railway system that would have been a paying proposition, instead of this enormous debt which we have to-day.
The leader of the Opposition says: "You already have 14,000 miles of Government

owned railways, why do you not experiment with that system?" I have tried to show, Mr. Speaker, how impossible it is to go on with this disorganized and disconnected system without the Grand Trunk to . back it up. The Canadian Pacific has a splendid organization in the eastern provinces; in the West there is a well rounded out s'ystem, thoroughly organized. We are all glad and proud to know that it is so successful, but we also must realize and appreciate this fact, that in the early days enormous sums of money and extensive land grants were made in order to place the Canadian Pacific railway upon a safe and sound footing.
Hon. members argue that the Grand Trunk should not be responsible for the Grand Trunk Pacific. I can hardly believe that any hon. member could support that contention, because I have under my hand the statement of the ex-Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and the statement of member after member on the other side in 1903 and 1904, showing what a splendid proposition they had'put before the people of Canada in the carrying out of the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme.
Other hon. members say: Wait until next session. This question was up in 1916, 1917 and 1918, and was thoroughly discussed from time to time, and the very proposition that we are voting on to-night or to-morrow has been before the country for the last sixteen months at least.

There are fifteen Government owned elevators, with a capacity of thirty-four,million bushels, all located along these railways, as well as the Canadian Northern elevators on their right of way, nine hundred and eighty-four in number, with a capacity of sixty-three million bushels- over a thousand elevators located along the right of way of these Government-owned roads. When this undertaking is consummated, the Intercolonial, the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern will be united in one system, and this system must remain entirely separate from the Canadian Pacific. The Canadian National railway must be under Canadian control and management, free from political interference. Let us give the trustees in charge of this great national undertaking the widest possible powers, and I have every confidence in the successful outcome of the proposition. The Government have presented the best possible solution of this problem. It is a safe, sound, sane, businesslike proposition, and I intend to give it my hearty support.

speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, another question: Is this the proper time to press this measure when the Finance Minister is calling upon the people of the country to lend money to the Government. This Government is like an ordinary man who wants money. If he desires to obtain money he has got to inspire confidence in the man from whom he demands it. Last year I went throughout my county and spoke in favour of the Victory Loan, and the contribution from Dorchester very largely exceeded the amount allotted to it by the Victory Loan Committee. This year I went again. Will I go back? I might go back providing the Minister of Finance shows us that this money will be properly spent, and not squandered and wasted in the scheme before the House at the present time. But what I can do is of no importance. I am a private member and do not claim to have much influence. But other people have. I would refer the Finance Minister to a letter which appeared in the Quebec papers; a letter not signed by a politician, not signed by an opponent of this Government, but signed by one of the most influential men in Canada, a former president of the Manufacturers' Association, a man who has built up in the city of Quebec one of the largest industries that we have-I am speaking of Hon. Mr. Amyot. Mr. Amyot subscribed to the last Victory Loan and subscribed generously, and this is the letter he writes:
To the Editor of Le Soleil,
Quebec.
Dear Sir,-
In this morning's Chronicle we are advised that the Ottawa Government has laid before the House the proposition for the purchase of the Grand Trunk railway, and that Mr. Smithers, the president, is prepared to accept conditions laid down by the Government. That is to say, that a pre-arranged scheme is being submitted to the House at the very moment when Sir Robert Borden is absent and when
the leader of the Opposition has no seat in the House, and at a time when the House was called for the unique purpose of ratifying the Peace Treaty, as well as to obtain for itself a second indemnity.
At this time, advantage is taken to rush through in a hurry a law for the purpose of taking over a fourth or a fifth railway system, to purchase the control of shares at a time when the country is staggering under the load of an excessive debt and burdened with all kinds of other troubles.
These gentlemen have the temerity to carry on this purchase at the time when they are endeavouring to float a national loan called a "Victory Loan." Vain words, no doubt, but in any case they call it a Victory Loan. I am of opinion that the country should refuse to subscribe anything whatsoever to this loan if the Government persists in its view that the Grand Trunk railway must *be acquired, and, in so far as I am concerned, I intend to give the example and will not subscribe one single cent. 1 have subscribed to loans made during the war and have done so generously. To the first loan $50,000, to the second $250,000, and to the third $500,000. Consequently I think that I have in the past done my bit, but I refuse to subscribe anything whatsoever to this last loan if it is the intention to administer the country's affairs in this reckless fashion; and if I have any advice to give it is, that my example should be generally followed throughout the country.
Thanking you, Sir, for the publication of this letter, I remain,
Tours very sincerely, George E. Amyot.
This letter cannot be ignored by the Government. As I said before, it is written by one of the most prominent men in Canada; and I think that the sentiments expressed are also shared by a great many business men throughout the country.
There is another reason, Mr. Speaker, why this measure should not be pressed. This Government has not the confidence of the peoplq. I say so, and I support my utterance with proofs that cannot be contradicted. A few months ago there was an election in Prince Edward Island. What was the result? The Provincial Government was defeated. Why? Because it was supported by the Union Government at Ottawa, But what is the use of speaking of Prince Edward Island, Mr. Speaker? I will refer to a province which is far more interesting to the hon. gentlman on the other side- the province of Ontario. The Hearst Government had been in power for many years; it had been supported in one general election; but the moment the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) lent his support to that Administration it was wiped out altogether. And the night the results came in I thought that my hon, friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid), who always had directed the old Tory machine in Ontario-this gentleman who knew where

to place some oil, for instance, when he went to Kingston to show to the people of that good town the ibenetfits of electing the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) by acclamation, as the papers have told us-this old political warrior of many battles would have carried the Tory machine to victory if it had not been for the reckless interference of his colleague, the President of the Council. But the moment the hon. gentleman interfered, like a misguided saint, he ruined the chances of the Hearst party altogether. If the electors of Prince Edward Island and Ontario receive in this fashion any party which is endorsed by the Union Government, can you imagine, Mr, Speaker, the disastrous results of a direct appeal from these gentlemen themselves?	If this
* Government had the confidence of the people why did they not put up a candidate in Quebec East, where there is an election this week, to explain to the people of my good province the benefits of their administration? I have not seen in this House for the last tfwo weeks the friendly face of the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder). I am sorry he is not here. But I would like to know, Mr. Speaker, if the Union Government has the confidence of the people, as was claimed yesterday by the President of the Council, why did not the Minister of Immigration put up a candidate of his own in the Province of Saskatchewan? They say they have the confidence of the people, Mr. Speaker. Well, the leader of our party was chosen by convention last summer, he offered himself to the electors of the County of Prince, and this Government, which has the confidence of the people, did not dare fight his election.

They have on their hands a number of white elephants that they would like to be rid of-somuch so, Mr. Speaker, that the question of nationalization is coming up again in that country, not only as regards the railways, but also as regards the mines. The Prime Minister, Mr. Lloyd George-and the member for Springfield will admit that he is a Liberal-has declared that the matter of the advisability of nationalization is of such grave importance that it will have to be decided by the people themselves. Hon. gentlemen opposite usually imitate what happens in England; why should they not make the same wise decision which the Prime Minister of England has made on this question?
They have had public ownership of railways in the United States. I challenge any member of this House to deny that the deficit on the railway in the United Stales under Government administration has not been a million and a half dollars , a day. Wliat, is it going to be here, judging from our experience in the past in connection with the Intercolonial?
Hon. gentlemen tell us that the administration of the national railways will be altogether outside of political patronage, "we have pledged ourselves to that." But this Government have made pledges in the



past which were never fulfilled-; the farming sections of Ontario remembered one pledge two days ago. This Government, Mr. Speaker, should bo serious. The President of the Council said yesterday:	"We have
to buy the Grand Trunk not on account of the failure of public ownership, but on account of the failure of private ownership." That was one of the main arguments put forwards by the Minister. The Canadian Northern failed as a private enterprise, and that is why the Government took it over. But what I cannot understand is why the Government, if they wish public ownership to be a success, leave in the hands of the same old gang who mal-admjnistered the Canadian Northern the administration of our national railways. If the man who was working for Mackenzie and Mann was not competent to administer a railway under private ownership where did he acquire new competency, additional talent, new administrative capacity, now that he works for the Government? If gentlemen go to the head office of the Canadian Northern in Toronto they will find there the same old faces of these political and railway buccaneers who robbed every Government in Canada; and they are still at. the same game. The President of the Council may wax eloquent, but these are cold facts that cannot be contradicted.
Who runs the Government railways? Whenever there is any trouble or any difficulty in this country we have only to go down to the Central Station to see on one of the sidings the private car of Mackenzie and Mann in which a Government official is receiving advice from these gentlemen. Everybody in Ottawa and throughout the country knows that. Yet these people talk about public ownership as being a public duty-"a patriotic duty", to use the expression of the President of the Council. Is it patriotic to ruin your country? If so, this is the first intimation I have had of it.
It is a new doctrine; it is a very modern theory. Mackenzie and Mann robbed and bled every Government in Canada. If this Government are sincere, they have one duty to perform, namely, to rid their system not only of Mackenzie and Mann who are the figurehead, but of the puppets who hide behind them. Giants in railroading have failed throughout the world in recent years; in the administration of railroads will this Government contend seriously that pygmies will succeed where giants have failed? Patronage is abolished! These railroads are going to be run in such a way that the administration of Canadian railways will

be cited throughout the world as a new wonder. Was it patronage or not, to give to the Hon. Mr. Carvell his reward and a $12,000 salary? Patronage abolished! In [DOT] my county, I have the example of a station .agent who was replaced after having been dismissed, because Hon. Mr. -Sevigny was running as a candidate, and he wired the general manager that, it was important that that station agent should still run the station because he had many relatives having votes in that constituency, and accordingly he was reinstated. But these gentlemen must be serious with the House of Commons and the country. Every Senator who is appointed is a political appoiptee and nothing else, and to remove that impression from my mind I would ask any minister of the Crown to explain to me why the appointment to the Senate concerning the county of Erontenac was not made before the elections were over. 'That is a very pertinent question.
The Government tell us that the main reason for this deal is necessity, it has to be done. Since when has it to be done? On the first September, when we met here, we were called upon only to put an end to the awful state of war which existed between us and Germany. I remember the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) making one of the most eloquent speeches ever delivered in this House when he called upon us as patriotic citizens of this country to put an end to the state of war. We were called upon for that purpose only, to give peace to the good men, women and children of Canada. We did that. The ministry was not satisfied. On September 20 this deal was not yet necessary; we did not hear anything about, it. Even on October 1, even on the 3rd, when the Acting Prime Minister	of	this country	(Sir GeorgeFoster) spoke in this House, he did	not disturb the	Government's
supporters who were packing their satchels and trunks in order to go home. It was not necessary then. But all of a sudden the atmosphere becomes loaded with clouds; the credit of this country is in danger! Again the Government proposes to the House of Commons a patriotic duty; we have to save the credit of Canada, says the President of the Council, all of a sudden. Save the credit of Canada! There is one way of saving the credit of Canada, and that is to prevent highway robbers and thieves from influencing the decisions of the Government

I bow to your decision, Sir. I say that it is the impression which wrongly exists in the minds of several people in Canada. The credit of this country has in no way been enhanced by the Canadian Northern deal; it was in no way enhanced by what we did last year; and I do not think it will be enhanced by the present proposal. It is necessary, say the Government, to help these railway companies. Since when has a company which is bankrupt, or on the way to bankruptcy, a claim on the generosity of this country? Other institutions in Canada have failed, have become bankrupt; have the Government interfered to give them financial help, to prevent them from failing? I will take a very recent example, the example of the Farmers' Bank in Ontario. That
11	p.m. institution failed, and hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House had promised their constituents relief. The Bill was thrown out by the Senate and the Government never introduced that Bill. Why? Because it is an altogether unsound principle to claim for any company a right to financial relief from the Government. LeP hon. gentlemen look at * what happened in the United States. Practically every important railway in the United States failed in the course of its existence. The American Government never interfered. When a railway failed, the same thing happened as when any other corporation failed. Since when have we, the people of Canada, become dealers in scrap and rags? This is a new role for a Government.
I am opposed to this Bill, not only because the time is not opportune and because the reasons given for the Bill do not justify its introduction or adoption, but because the method indicated by the Government is wrong. Why should we have arbitration? We had an example of what arbitration meant to the people of Canada. The Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) when he was chairman of the Railway Board, declared that the Canadian Northern stock was absolutely worthless.
80}	I
Nevertheless, the arbitrators who were named by the Government decided that a stock which was worth absolutely nothing, not one cent, was to cost the people of Canada the enormous sum of $10,800,000. We, the representatives of the people, have no right to constitute a tribunal on the same basis as that, which meant'such a tremendous loss to the country in connection with taking over the Canadian Northern. Are we going to have the same experts to determine the value of this stock? I have nothing to say against these gentlemen, but if my memory serves me right, one of those who sat on the Canadian Northern arbitration board was the Chief Justice of the province of Ontario, and he again is named in this Bill to choose one of the arbitrators, together with the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court and the senior judge of the Exchequer Court of Canada.

If I go ahead the way I am it will be going ahead differently from the minister because my course will be straight. I say we have no right to put in the hands of these, gentlemen the decision of suah an important question after the way the Canadian people were treated at their hands a year or so ago. That tribunal gave over $10,000,000 to Mackenzie and Mann and their friends for a stock which was absolutely valueless, and the present Minister of Finance declared so himself. What is going to happen so far as the Grand Trunk is concerned we do not know. The sinister influences which were exercised in connection with the Canadian Northern still prevail. We know those men. Unfortunately for Canada they are still alive. They are watching these proceedings. The papers in Canada which have supported the present Administration for years, papers which put the present Administration into power, are protesting against this Bill and against the methods employed to take over the Grand Trunk. I hope that when we are in committee on the Bill, if it is not withdrawn altogether, it will be decided by the Government that no arbitration award shall be binding on the people of this country until ratified by the Parliament of Canada. Why should we divest ourselves of our responsibility? Why should three gentlemen, no matter who they are, impose on this

country an expenditure of millions of dollars? The constitutional theory on this point is very simple-no taxation without representation. I need not recall the long struggle in England and in Canada for the adoption and sanction of this .constitutional principle. We have it. The members of the House of Commons, the sole representatives of the people, have no right to give to three judges, no matter who they are, the right of taxing the Canadian people, especially when that taxation amounts to millions and millions of dollars.
I will conclude these remarks by saying that the responsibility of the Government in a constitutional .country is very heavy The role played by a minister is very noble and very high. The trust that the people put in the ministers is a trust that should be respected. The. Canadian people have entrusted these gentlemen with the protection and the safeguarding of their interests, financial, national and otherwise. These gentlemen are simply the stewards of the people. If they read the Gospel, as I have no doubt the President of the Council does every day, they will see tint our Lord speaks in very stern words of the responsibility of stewardship. He painted the duties of stewardship as the most binding that a man can have imposed upon him. Stewards of the people, you have no right to squander one cent of the public moneys. Not the smallest fraction of money should be squandered or wasted. The Canadian people are watching, and I hope that some time the sun will rise on the day of reckoning for these gentlemen. I have no doubt that when that day comes, not the Canadian Northern, not the Grand Trunk, not the Grand Trunk Pacific, or any of their railways will prevent them from being removed from their seats to your right, Mr. Speaker, to the seats on your left in this House.

speechtext:
If the debate from this on is to be a serious discussion of the resolution before the Chair, it is imperative that very little time or attention he paid to the speech of the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon). The speech he has just delivered was characteristic of him. in that it was replete With what might be called clever turns of language, and also characteristic of him in that it was absolutely barren of everything else. There may be some success in controversy in this House if there is substance, relevant substance, to an address, even in the absence of candour, and candour in a speech in the absence of material facts or substance is always aocept-

able and welcome; but a speech that is lacking in both is not likely to live very long in the memory of hon. members.
I noted as time went on, two or three references the hon. member made which had some remote bearing on the resolution we are now discussing. I was interested as well without noting any relevance to the subject, in the appeal he made, a very touching appeal, on behalf of the returned soldiers of this country and their families, and I could not help but reflect on the sweet and enduring gratification it will bring to all the soldiers arid heroes of our country when they learn that their champion in this House is now the hon. member for Dorchester. He had all the resources of his mind marshalled to attack the arbitration that took place on the subject of the Canadian Northern railway shares. I do not know whether his language in that regard was any more extravagant than his language relative to the Bill before Parliament. There is this however about the effect of the hon. member's opinion, that if there were any serious minded members of this House who had any honest doubts as to the wisdom of his course in supporting this legislation, these doubts would be set at rest when he finds that the measure meets with the envenomed hostility of the hon. member for Dorchester.
As to the arbitration that took place two years ago words failed the hon. member to properly characterize that policy. He thinks that any course on the part of the Government in regard to large railway systems that does not permit the onward, or downward, march of liquidation is reprehensible in every respect. There is in ^ such a course, he, sayls, a violation of responsibility and an utter ignoring of our duties to the people. Let railway systems, like everything else, go into liquidation and all is well! That is the way it has been and the way it ought to be! I was in this House when the gentleman whose memory the hon. member for Dorchester affects to revere was leading the Liberal party. If the hon. gentleman refers to the recordri of this House at the time when this Parliament was faced with the alternative of the Canadian Northern going into liquidation, a system less in magnitude than the Grand Trunk, he will see that that leader stood up in Parliament and warned us that it was our duty not to allow liquidation to take place. He warned this House that the duty before it was to arrest the progress of liquidation in the name of and

for the sake of the credit of this country and for the dearest interests of Canada. Not only did the leader of that day use such words and warn the Government accordingly, but his ex-Minieter of Railways, Hon. G. P. Graham, now not in Par-liaament, was even more emphatic than the then leader of the Opposition in chiding Parliament for ever thinking of liquidation as to the Canadian Northern system because it meant more in loss than this country could hope to gain thereby. If liquidation was a thing unthinkable for the Canadian Northern railway is the argument not equally applicable to the Grand Trunk? All the arguments used by Sir Wilfrid Laurier relative to the Canadian Northern railway apply equally, identically and with redoubled force to the subject now before this House. But logic is lost on an intellect under the sway of passion such as that possessed by the hon. member for Dorchester. Liquidation is right; public ownership is wrong. With the Canadian Northern liquidation was wrong but public ownership was right.
When the subject was before Parliament the Opposition of that time, within whose ranks were many hon. members opposite, moved a resolution calling for the public ownership of the Canadian Northern system, calling for arbitration as to the value of the stock in the Canadian Northern with a maximum of $30,000,000, the very course that we afterwards pursued except that we reduced the maximum to $10,000,000. I heard this subject referred to by the present temporary leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) the other day. " Yes," he said, " we did in 1914 support a resolution moved by Dr. T'ugsley, calling for the taking over of the CanadianNorthern Railway system by means of the ownership of the stock at a value to be defined by arbitration and calling for the fixing of a maximum of $30,000,000 as the value of that stock. But, "he said," that was before we loaned them $35,000,000; as soon as we loaned them $35,000,000, they had $5,000,000 more than our maximum and therefore the maximum could not stand." I hardly know how to attack a position of that sort. As if the value of the stock of the system was depreciated by the fact that we loaned them $35,000,000. The $35,000,000 was a loan to the company. It was opposed because it would help the stockholders. How would it help the stockholders if it ruined the stock? If it had any effect on the stock it
would raise the value of the stock. Though the stock which, without that raise, was to have under their plan a maximum value in arbitration of $30,000,000, still in the opinion of hon. gentlemen opposite there is robbery of Canada if the stock having this raise is arbitrated at a maximum of $10,000,000. I do not hear the mutterings of the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) for which I should be grateful.
We have had abundant and repeated witness of the truism that there is no use whatever in taking the advice in any respect of hon. gentlemen opposite because the moment we take that advice they deny its parenthood and assail their own ideas. Liquidation, let me repeat, was the agreed upon and recorded policy of hon. gentlemen opposite in relation to the Canadian Northern Railway system. Arbitration of the value of the shares was right and public ownership was right. Will any hon, gentleman tell me why liquidation was wrong in connection with the Canadian Northern and public ownership and arbitration right, and liquidation right and public ownership and arbitration wrong in respect to the Grand Trunk? The exigencies of political position are very great and drive public men into strange paths; and in proportion as the leadership is vacillating these exigencies become more repeated and more difficult.
I did not rise to refer particularly to the remarks of the hon. member for Dorchester. I was not able to be in the House when the ^hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) was making his speech the other day, but I took occasion as I sat in my seat to-night to read it, and I thought I would be lacking somewhat in my duty- I had almost said to posterity-if I did not put on record a gem that I found in this speech. It is full of them, all of them just about, although not quite approaching in ludicrousness the specimen I am now going to treat. There is indeed scarcely a paragraph in the speech but against which the same attack could be made that I am going to make against this, but time prevents me from going over the other paragraphs with a like purpose. The hon. gentleman was endeavouring to show the burden that was going to fall upon Canada by way of annual charges as a result of taking over the Grand Trunk system and incorporating it with the Canadian National railways. He said first that the outstanding indebtedness of the system was $552,556,019. I find here in the blfip-book he was relying on, a figure

There is this difference between me and the hon. gentleman. When I argue what common sense is I precede it by some reason, I do not simply pronounce it as from high Heaven and say, "This is final, let it go."
The hon. gentleman then moves his resolution which says: We cannot go on and decide this question in the closing days of the session. Well, what makes the session close? Is it not when we get through? How is it that we could decide this subject better if .something else followed? If we have only this to consider, and this is the last business, have we not more time for its consideration than if we had some other things to consider? What particular

advantage would it be to us in our deliberations on this Bill to know there were some other Bills to follow? The hon. gentleman's resolution in effect says, there would be great advantage ! We are not asking him to go home,

we are not asking any one to go home. From the moment we had reason to believe that we were likely to secure the culmination of the negotiations we invited every one to stay. That was our plain duty, and that is our invitation today. No effort has been spared on the part of the Government to urge that hon. members both of this House and the Senate remain at their posts, and without hurry, without agitation, without being driven in any way quietly, calmly, and deliberately to think this thing out and decide what is best to be done on behalf of the people of Canada.
