Well, naturally the taking over of a large railway system adds to our obligations and to our responsibilities; there is no doubt about that. Canada is under obligations to the Grand Trunk shareholders, who, in the early days, with but small government assistance, and in competition with the railways of the United States with their vastly greater resources, built up the first Canadian railway system. In later times the company has had further to meet the competition of heavily subsidized Canadian rivals. And it cannot be said that at any stage of its history the shareholders have obtained excessive profits on their enterprise. On the whole we recommend that, on condition of the surrender by the Grand Trunk Company of their entire share capital, guaranteed, preferred, and ordinary, the trustees grant a certain annuity, charged as a working expense on the whole undertaking of the Dominion Railway Company, for the first seven years, increasing at the termination of that period by something like 40 or 50 per cent.
We have left the figures blank as there will be questions. of cash in hand, value of stores, etc., .which- must make the precise figures subject to negotiation.
But our meaning is that the first figure should be a moderate but substantial percentage of $3,600,000'-
Now, during the. course of the reading of that the Minister of Railways interjected: "That is what we are doing," and the hon. gentleman went on to explain:
"A moderate percentage of $3,600,000." I would like to know from the Minister of Railways where under this bargain he makes an annual payment of a moderate percentage of $3,600,000.
Mr. J. D. Reid:	There is the $2,500,000.

Mr. J. D. Reid:	This was to be in addition
to that.
Mr. McKenzie:	This report does not say so.
This report says that the company have to deliver up everything they have.

Mr. J. D. Reid:	No, it does not.
Mr. McKenzie:	That is the suggestion here.
They have to deliver, holus bolus, everything they have from common stock up and then the Government comes in and makes an allowance upon the basis of $3,600,000, not the whole but a moderate or substantial percentage of the amount. That is the suggestion of the Drayton-Acworth commission and that is the only authority which the Government have to-day.
The hon.1 gentleman was telling this House that the suggestion of the Drayton-Acworth Commission was that there should be paid a moderate but substantial percentage of $3,600,000, against not the preference stock, the guaranteed stock and the common stock, but against all the bonds on which the interest is from seven to eight millions, and against -the guaranteed preference stocks and common stocks as well. One reading of the Drayton-Acworth report by anybody at all will make it clear that the report not only intended to say but said distinctly: "Take it subject to these bonds and pay to the stockholders a moderate but substantial percentage of $3,600,000, and add to whatever you pay during the first few years by forty or fifty per cent later on." Surely, that is clear.

speechtext:
In regard to this case the hon. gentleman's mistakes were real errors and might be forgiven. I am not so sure that having regard to his whole course as leader in the conduct of other debates there has not been something to be ashamed of.
Referring again to the apprehensions of the hon. member for Royal (Mr. H. H. McLean) the obligations which we assume are set out distinctly in the now historic report which has been before this Parliament for over two years, to which our policy is securely anchored, on which it is built and by which it is justified. We are now negotiating, as the report recommends, as to just the proportion of that $3,600,000 we shall pay. We are compelled to negotiate by way of arbitration for the simple reason that we cannot agree. We take the company's properties, subject to their obligations which the company has in normal times, and up until the last year or so, always discharged out- of its earnings; and we assume a proportion of what they have regularly paid to their shareholders. That is the situation. We do that not because we want to, not because we are running out into the highways and by-ways to see what railways we can gather into our system,

that is not the spirit behind the Government's * policy,-we do that because we find ourselves in this position:	We
find ourselves with a system of railways truncated and divided East from West, a system of railways that by its very composition cannot be a complete or successful system. But more than that we do it because we find' ourselves saddled with the burden of operating at tremendous loss two great railways which private companies found themselves unable to operate-the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental. The Grand Trunk Pacific operated last year at a Joss of $10,300,000 odd and the Transcontinental at a loss of something I think, between five and six millions. These are two roads which were built in
[Mr. Meighen. J
my judgment, without any justification. They were badly founded in business sense from the commencement. But if they had any justification, however meagre, however inadequate, it was this:	that they were
extensions of, .and part of, and to be operated with, the Grand Trunk- system. Those two railways operated not in conjunction with .and as part of .the Grand Trunk system could scarcely be said to be railways at all, operation of them I repeat, disjointed from that system, is unjustified on any principle of business or on .any principle of national common-sense.
They must be operated in the very body-commercial of that system if they are to serve the purposes for which railways are built. How are we going to do that if we do not acquire this railway? How are we going to do that if we do not stretch but and make the system what it was intended to be? How can we get any even moderately adequate value out of the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Transcontinental? We must unite it up with the great system, of which it was built to be a portion, an auxiliary, an extension and integral part. The hon. member refers to the possibility -I have heard of it more than once-of some traffic agreement that we might make with the Grand Trunk that would make that system serve the purposes intended to be served toward the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental. If such an agreement were in the interest of the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk would have been before us to make the agreement long before this; indeed, it would have been in existence long ago. Ah, we are told, you can force it on them. So, perhaps we could, by holding them to their Grand Trunk Pacific obligations; strictly, we might. But here is -a company that as it is to-day cannot stand up, cannot at all events continue long under present conditions. How then is it to continue, after we have forced upon it an agreement that binds it against its interest to serve the Tanscontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip

speechtext: At the last annual meeting of the Grand Trunk shareholders held in London, England, in March, Mr. Smithers is reported to have stated to the shareholders that he made an offer to the Government for an absolute interchange of traffic as between the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk system and to operate that .system at cost. Will the minister enlighten the House as to the correctness of that?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Yes, they to operate one end /and we to operate the other. A moment's consideration of the proposal would convince the hon. member-I do not know whether he has read it or not-that such an idea would manifestly not be in the interest of Canada. They were to get the good and we take the bad. But that is not the traffic agreement I have in mind. A traffic agreement that we forced upon the Grand Trunk railway would make us answerable to the Grand Trunk railway for the penalties which that railway might suffer as a result. Could we answer them by saying: We will not assist you, although we forced upon you a traffic agreement which makes your road subservient to ours and help to make our road pay. Before I leave that, let me repeat that we are asked to do that with a road that is now at the door of the Government for assistance; that now under present conditions is meeting with all manner of difficulties in traversing its path. But we have had traffic agreements with the Grand Trunk; we have had an agreement for interchange at Montreal with the Intercolonial, [DOT]and what has been the result? Any man in this House who understands railway business will know that, unless there is a definite selfish purpose to be served by a road in living up to traffic agreement, that traffic agreement will never serve the other road. There are a thousand evasions ooen, all manner of them, and you cannot follow them up. Have we ever been able to do so with the traffic agreement we had? It has been one continual process of dispute and arbitration ever since it was entered into and with no satisfactory results, and that was a traffic agreement only as to a small specific matter of local interchange. But a traffic agreement that is intended practically to make one big system operate in unison with another, especially a traffic agreement in any way contracted under duress, is wholly impracticable and ineffectual. That is our position.
It is worth while to add that if such an arrangement were in practice by any means made effective, it would have the practical result of bringing this system in any event under the wing of the Government subject to Government dictation and entailing Government responsibility. It would have all the disadvantages and none of the merits of complete government ownership, operation and control. Therefore, the fact is not that we are eagerly seeking after new responsibilities; we are not; we are not in a financial position to seek new responsibilities that we can legitimately avoid; the
fact is that we find ourselves in
12	p.m. a position at once onerous and grave-a position that can be relieved and improved only by the acquisition of a system that makes our own system real; that makes our present system an operating possibility and at probable success. That is why we take the course that we do. I have heard many objections and I know there are many hon. members who, if they were given a choice between assuming these responsibilities and simply *standing aside without any responsibilities at all, would gladly take the second alternative

many an hon. member on both sides would, I believe, gladly do that-but we are not in that position. We cannot get out of responsibilities, it is only a case of choosing which class of responsibility we shall assume, and .any criticism of these proposals that is not accompanied by an alternative proposal that will meet the stern necessities binding on us at this time is of no value by way of criticism. It is a waste of words and should pass by us as the idle wind. We have been addressed by prominent business men, as prominent indeed, as tire very respectable gentleman (Mr. Amyot) quoted by the honourable member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon). We have been addressed from many quarters, I feel, by big business even which seems on this subject to be allied with honourable gentlemen opposite. We have been addressed with objections to government ownership in theory, principle and practice and all the rest of it. But we have never been addressed from big business or little business, from politician or stateman or newspaper or any pne else with any workable alternative that we could put in place of the proposals which we now venture to advance. Standing _ squarely and facing these facts, is it not the duty of Parliament to support the Government in the course we are pursuing? Is it not the duty of honourable members of this House to make clear to the people of this country our real position, not an enviable position, it is true, but a very real position that we are now in-and show them what is undoubtedly the truth, namely, that we are making the best of a bad situation, seeking to the best of our capacity as representatives of the people to take a course in the best and final interest of all?
